activity: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
knowledge_domain: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
fact: In 1936 the Literary Digest poll collected about 2.4 million responses yet predicted that Alf Landon would beat Franklin Roosevelt, who then won in a landslide.
story:
The line inside the gymnasium moved in stops and starts, and Rachel counted the people she had already approached: eleven, of whom seven had agreed to answer her four questions. Her clipboard felt heavier than it should have. She had promised Ms. Brennan a real exit poll for the school paper, with actual numbers, and the paper went to print Thursday.

"Eleven people." Easton had found her by the water fountains, holding his phone like evidence at a trial. "My poll has six thousand responses. Six thousand, Rachel. You're going to write a story on eleven?"

"Twelve now. That man in the windbreaker just filled it out."

"Twelve." He turned the screen toward her. "I posted it Monday night. Six thousand people can't be wrong."

"Six thousand people who follow your account," she said. "That's not the same as six thousand people."

He laughed, short, the way he did when he thought someone was dodging. "It's called a sample size. Bigger is better. Even Ms. Brennan says that."

Ms. Brennan was standing near the check-in table, directing an elderly voter toward the correct precinct letter, and Rachel decided not to pull her into it yet. She went back to the line instead, because that was the work, and the work was all she could defend. A woman with a cane waved her off. A man in a delivery uniform answered all four questions and then said, "You know it's a secret ballot, right? I could be lying to you." Rachel wrote his answers down anyway and added a small question mark beside them, which felt like the most honest thing on the page.

By noon she had thirty-one responses, and the count was close, sixteen to fifteen, so close that she could feel the number trembling every time she looked at it. Easton came back with two classmates, Dakota among them, and set his phone on the folding table where the poll workers kept the sign-in sheets. "Tell her," he said to Dakota. "Six thousand responses. My candidate's up by nine points."

"Up by nine," Rachel repeated. She had read something, late the night before, chasing exactly this argument down, and now she reached for her bag and found the torn-out library page. "In 1936, the Literary Digest poll collected about 2.4 million responses, and it predicted Alf Landon would beat Roosevelt. Roosevelt won in a landslide."

Dakota frowned. "Two point four million. That's not a poll, that's a census."

"So the biggest sample ever was the most wrong," Rachel said. "It happens. I don't fully know why yet, but I know it happened." She looked at Easton. "So no, your six thousand doesn't settle it by itself."

Easton took the page from her, read it twice, and his jaw worked. "Fine," he said finally. "Then your thirty-one people settle even less. You can't exculpate your little clipboard by convicting my phone."

"That's fair," Rachel said, and meant it, and it surprised her that it came out steady. "Mine doesn't settle anything either. But mine came from that line, not from people who already agreed with me enough to click a link you posted."

Dakota leaned on the table. "So both of you are saying the other one's numbers are broken. And nobody's saying what would make them not broken."

"Random," Rachel said slowly, assembling it as she spoke. "Mine isn't random, it's whoever walks past me before noon. His isn't random either. Maybe that matters more than how many." She could feel the shape of something she couldn't yet prove, and she didn't pretend otherwise. "And the margin of error on thirty-one people is huge. Sixteen to fifteen is basically a tie with a costume on."

Easton was quiet for a moment, thumbing the edge of the library page. Ms. Brennan passed behind them carrying a box of pens and said nothing, which Rachel understood as its own kind of permission.

"There's something else," Dakota said. "The two of you have been at each other since Monday, and now you're basically agreeing. It's like a symbiosis where you each need the other one to be half wrong."

"That's germane to my problem, actually," Rachel said. "Because I have to write something by Thursday, and the truest thing I can write is that the race is close and neither of us knows." She looked at Easton. "Co-author. Both numbers, both problems, one article."

Easton folded the page and put it in his jacket pocket instead of handing it back. "I keep the byline alphabetized," he said. "E before R."

"You wish," Rachel said, and turned back toward the line, where the next voter was already reaching for her pencil.

activity: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
knowledge_domain: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
fact: Plain-language guidance recommends the active voice, in which the subject does the action, as in 'I missed the deadline', because it makes clear who did what.
story:
Coralie sat at the kitchen computer with the bakery's apology draft open and the cursor blinking after the seventh word. Three lines down, in the middle of the paragraph, sat the phrase she had written on instinct: "mistakes were made regarding your daughter's birthday cake." The customer, Mrs. Okafor, had ordered it for a Saturday pickup, and Coralie had entered the date for the following Saturday, and the cake had not existed when Mrs. Okafor arrived with her niece and a box of candles.

The draft had taken her twenty minutes, and it was polite, and it was wrong in some way she could not name. She read it aloud under her breath, the way Mr. Takahashi had told them to do in tenth grade, and the sentence went soft in her mouth, like something dissolving.

She flashed back to that classroom, October, rain on the windows. Mr. Takahashi had put two sentences on the board and asked which one they would rather hear from a friend who owed them money. "The money was spent," he read, flat, and then, differently, "I spent the money," and half the class had laughed, and he had said only, "Notice which one you trust." He never said why. She had written it in the margin of her notebook anyway, next to a doodle of a fish, and forgotten it until now.

She opened a search bar and typed "how to write an apology to a customer." Most of what came back was promotional and vague, but one page, from a plain-language project, was plain itself. It recommended the active voice, in which the subject does the action, as in "I missed the deadline," because it makes clear who did what. Coralie read the sentence twice, then looked back at her own draft. Mistakes were made. Nobody had made them, apparently. They had simply occurred, like weather.

Her phone buzzed against the desk. Cailyn, from the group chat with just the two of them in it: "did you tell mrs o yet? also can you take my sunday shift PLEASE my cousin's confirmation." Cailyn wanted the shift covered, and she had been angling for it since Wednesday, complimenting Coralie's stamina, offering her the good station by the ovens, laughing a little too brightly at everything Coralie said. Coralie typed back that she would think about Sunday, and before she could close the chat, Cailyn called.

"You're still on the computer," Cailyn said. "I can hear you not typing."

"I'm writing the email to Mrs. Okafor. The cake email."

"Okay, keep it short. Say the order was delayed. Say arrangements are being made for a replacement. My manager at the shoe store calls that professional distance."

Coralie looked at the starter tub she had carried home from the bakery, the one fermenting on the counter in its cloudy jar, giving off its faint sour warmth. She thought about distance. "I don't think distance is what she wants," she said. "She stood in the shop for ten minutes while I searched the system. She knows exactly who entered the date."

"So? You'll get in trouble."

"Maybe. But she deserves to know it was me. The guidance says the active voice, where the subject does the action. Like, 'I missed the deadline.' It makes clear who did what."

"That sounds like a great way to get written up," Cailyn said, but she said it slower, and Coralie could hear her turning it over.

Coralie deleted the sentence. In its place she wrote, "I entered the wrong pickup date, and I am sorry. I missed the deadline for your daughter's cake." Then, because an apology that admitted fault still owed something, she wrote that she would like to offer a replacement at no charge, and that if Mrs. Okafor preferred a refund instead, Coralie would process it the same day. She read the paragraph aloud again. It held its shape. She moved the truculent feeling in her chest, the part that wanted to hide, to one side, the way she moved the wet cloth off the starter jar every morning, and pressed send before it could ferment into something she would rewrite.

The reply came forty minutes later, while she was washing the jar's rim. Mrs. Okafor wrote that she appreciated the honesty, that her daughter had cried but that nine-year-olds recover, and that she would take the replacement, and could Coralie write the message on the cake herself. Coralie sat back down at the computer and opened the order form. She typed "Happy Birthday Amara" into the decorator's notes field, then deleted it and typed, "Sorry I'm late, Amara. Love, the bakery lady who owes you." Her phone buzzed again, Cailyn asking about Sunday one more time. Coralie picked it up and, still looking at the order form, started her reply with "Okay, but you owe me."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Isaac Newton arranged the colors of the spectrum into a circle in his 1704 book Opticks, an early version of the color wheel artists use today.
story:
Carter had commandeer an old door leaning behind the craft shed, and by noon it lay across two sawhorses with his pencil grid already faint on it. The camp director's injunction had been posted on the mess hall board for a week: no more hand-lettered cardboard signs, something permanent for the lake path, something that would survive rain. He was to paint the trail marker, arrows and distances to the dock, the fire pit, the canoe launch. Eighteen campers would walk past it every day, which meant every color choice would be public whether he liked it or not.

The problem was the blue. He had planned the whole scheme around it, a deep lake blue for the background, and then discovered the supply shelf held only a bruised, grayish tube that dried the color of a storm drain. He sat on the sawhorse staring at it while Jeevan sorted brushes into jars behind him, and the morning heat pressed down through the pines and settled on the back of his neck.

"You could mix it," Jeevan said. "Green and something."

"Green makes it worse. It's already halfway to green."

Alexanne came around the shed with a popsicle stick in her mouth and her sketchbook under her arm. She looked at the door, at the test swatches drying in a row along the edge, blue after blue after disappointing blue. "You're going at it like a hammer," she said. "What's across from blue on the color wheel?"

"Orange. Obviously. But I need blue."

"So make the orange do the work." She flipped her sketchbook open to a page of watercolor studies, all done in flat gray with a single warm element, a red scarf, a yellow window. "Everything around the blue changes what the blue is. Put orange next to your gray tube and it'll read cold. It'll read lake."

Carter didn't answer right away. It went against something in him, the idea that a color should be what it was on its own, that if the tube said blue the painting should be blue. But he had spent two days on that belief and had twelve muddy swatches to show for it. He mixed orange instead, a sharp cadmium, and laid a band of it along the bottom of the door, then dragged the gray-blue above it. The blue deepened the moment the orange touched its edge. It was almost a trick. It bothered him a little that it was almost a trick.

"Who figured that out anyway," he said, half to himself. "That opposites make each other stronger."

Jeevan came and stood over the door with a brush dripping in his hand. "Newton, actually. The color wheel. He took the colors of the spectrum and bent them into a circle in his Opticks. 1704. Physicist, not a painter." He said it lightly, the way he reported everything, and went back to his jars.

Carter looked at the door for a long moment, at the embryonic marker taking shape under his hands, arrows not yet drawn, lettering still only penciled. He had assumed the wheel belonged to painters, that it had risen out of their studios the way recipes rise out of kitchens. Instead it had started with someone arranging light into a shape, and painters had borrowed it after. Which meant the thing Alexanne was telling him, that context could define a color, sat on the same shelf as his instinct that a color should stand alone, and both had a claim. He wasn't sure yet which he actually believed, or whether he had to choose. He was sure only that the blue looked better than anything he had mixed on purpose.

He penciled a small circle in the corner of the door, then drew a line through its center and labeled one end blue and the other orange, as much to remember the argument as the technique. When he got to the real arrows he would decide whether the marker stayed honest to the gray tube or let the orange carry it. For now he taped off the bottom band and brushed a clean edge along it, and Alexanne leaned over and licked the last of her popsicle stick clean.

"If you're putting that circle on the sign," she said, "put a date under it. People will want to know how old the idea is."

"Seventeen oh-four," he said, and printed it small, in pencil, below the line.

activity: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
knowledge_domain: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
fact: Sociologist Robert K. Merton's 1936 essay 'The Unanticipated Consequences of Purposive Social Action' listed causes of unintended consequences, including ignorance, error and focusing on immediate interests over long-term ones.
story:
Luca slid the library book back onto the shelf without looking at it, because the important thing was happening four tables away, where Keiran was explaining to Adrien, in a voice pitched just loud enough to be overheard, that the cafeteria plan had not failed. "It's a setback," Keiran said. "We removed the trays, people took less food, waste went down. That part worked."

"The part that didn't work," Adrien said, "is that half the school now buys chips from the corner store because the lunch lines got so long nobody eats. So there's a pile of chip bags in the parking lot every day instead of food waste in the cafeteria." He tore the corner off a napkin and folded it into a smaller and smaller square, a sullen little accordion of paper.

Mr. Gill, who supervised the library two afternoons a week, had paused near the returns cart. "Council meets Thursday," he said. "I'll ask the same question I asked today. Why did nobody see it coming? You don't have to have an answer, but you should try to have one." He went back to scanning barcodes, and the fluorescent light extruded his long shadow across the carpet, all the way to the leg of Luca's table.

Luca had, in fact, voted for the plan, which was the part he had not said out loud yet. He typed "why do plans go wrong" into the library catalogue, then "consequences," then, after a moment of wondering whether he was even asking the right question, "unintended." One result came back: a bound journal volume from 1936, shelved in the section nobody visited, where the radiators ticked like a slow clock.

He carried it to the table and opened it flat between his elbows. The essay had a title long enough to be its own sentence: "The Unanticipated Consequences of Purposive Social Action," by a sociologist named Robert K. Merton. He read the first page twice. Merton had sat down, apparently, and tried to list the reasons good plans turn strange, and the reasons were almost insultingly simple. One was ignorance. One was error. One was what happened when people focused on immediate interests instead of long-term ones. Luca caught himself smiling at the word immediate, because that was exactly it, exactly the shape of the thing the council had done.

"Found something?" Keiran said, drifting over with his backpack still on one shoulder.

Luca turned the volume around. "Nineteen thirty-six. This guy Merton basically wrote our Thursday meeting." He tapped the page. "We wanted the waste numbers down before the end of term. That was the immediate thing. We never asked what happens next month." He was careful, even as he said it, not to dress it up as proof. It wasn't a syllogism, he thought; it didn't march from premise to premise and arrive somewhere unavoidable. It was more like weather. You could see the conditions, and still not know if it would rain.

Adrien came over too and read with his hands in his pockets, bending from the waist like a question mark. "So ignorance and error are on the list too. Which one were we?"

"That's the part I can't decide," Luca said. "We didn't know about the lines getting longer. But we could have timed them. We just didn't." He wondered whether that made it ignorance or error or something Merton hadn't bothered to name, and whether the difference even mattered to the kids sweeping chip bags off the asphalt.

Keiran sat down across from him, finally, and pulled the volume closer. "So Thursday, we say what? Sorry, we were ignorant?"

"We say we focused on the immediate," Luca said. "And then we time the lines before whatever we try next." He copied the title of the essay onto the back of his hand, because he had left every notebook he owned at home, which was, he supposed, its own small instance of error. Outside the tall window the October light was going amber, and somewhere near the printers a boy was feeding paper into a jammed tray, pulling each crumpled sheet back out and smoothing it flat before trying again.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: Earth's surface gives off heat as infrared radiation; greenhouse gases absorb much of it and re-emit it in all directions, including back down, which warms the lower atmosphere.
story:
Julia spread the printout on the kitchen table and weighted its corners with a mug and two forks. The graph showed carbon dioxide from 1900 to the present, a line that climbed in small jagged steps, and beneath it a question from the practice sheet: explain, in your own words, why the lower atmosphere warms. She had two days before the placement exam that would decide whether she started college in the remedial science block or the regular one, and the exam apparently assumed she understood things her high school had never quite finished teaching.

Her first draft read: greenhouse gases form a layer that blocks heat from leaving. She looked at it, then at the diagram beside the graph, arrows curving up from a drawn ground and arrows bending back down. A layer that blocks heat would be simpler. She crossed it out.

Kailyn called at eight. "Tell me you're not doing the sheet."

"I'm doing the sheet. Come over. Bring Casey if he's awake."

They arrived within half an hour, Casey carrying leftover chips, Kailyn carrying her own sheet, blank except for her name. They pulled chairs up to the table and Julia turned the diagram so it faced them. "Okay, so. Say the ground is warm. It's giving off heat. Not the sun's heat coming in, its own heat, going out."

"Like a radiator," Casey said.

"Sure, like a radiator. It goes out as infrared radiation." She tapped the arrows rising from the drawn ground. "Now here's where I had it wrong all afternoon. I thought the greenhouse gases just bounce it back, like a mirror."

"Isn't that what the sheet says?" Kailyn leaned over the page.

"No. Look at the arrows. They don't bounce. The gas molecules absorb the heat. They take it in." She drew a small circle in the margin with arrows radiating from it on every side, up, down, sideways. "And then they re-emit it. In all directions. Some of it goes up and out, but some of it goes back down, toward the ground."

Casey took a chip and chewed slowly, watching the diagram. "So the ground gets its own heat handed back to it."

"And the lower atmosphere warms," Julia said. "That's the whole thing. The gas doesn't block the heat, it absorbs it and re-emits it, and some of the re-emitted heat goes back down." She wrote a sentence along the bottom of her draft and read it aloud as she went. "Earth's surface gives off heat as infrared radiation; greenhouse gases absorb much of it and re-emit it in all directions, including back down, which warms the lower atmosphere."

Kailyn copied it onto her own sheet, then stopped. "Wait. All directions? Not just down?"

"All directions, including down. That's why it's not a mirror." Julia set her pen down. "Ms. Hughes would have explained this in ten minutes last spring if I'd gone to office hours instead of pretending the unit didn't exist."

"You compartmentalize," Kailyn said. "You put the stuff you don't get in a box and act like the box is in another building."

"It was in another building. My brain, second drawer." Julia pulled the graph back toward herself. The sawtooth line rose and rose, dipped, rose again, year over year. She traced one of the small dips with her fingertip. "These dips repeat. Every year, same shape."

"Summer in the northern hemisphere," Casey said. "Plants take in carbon when they grow. More land up here, more plants."

"So the planet breathes." Julia said it flatly, then decided she meant it. "But the breathing doesn't level out. Each year's peak is above the last one. That's what a century of this looks like." She turned the graph toward the window, where the porch light made the paper translucent, and the line showed through like a scratch in glass.

They worked until ten, Kailyn filling both sides of her sheet, Casey asking questions Julia could mostly answer and writing down the ones she couldn't, which turned out to be a longer list than she expected. How much is much of it, she had said to the ceiling, and Casey had shrugged, and she had written the question in the margin with the word uncertain underlined twice, because her mother had always said that marking what you don't know is half of knowing anything, and because the exam, whatever else it did, could not fault her for honesty she couldn't back up.

At the door, Kailyn held up her sheet. "You realize you taught this better than it was ever taught to us."

"I got it wrong first. That's the only reason it's right now." Julia folded her own sheet into thirds and put it in the pocket of her jacket, which hung on the back of a chair, which she would carry upstairs, later, past the kitchen window where the porch light stayed on all night for no one.

Casey paused on the steps. "So tomorrow, the exam. You ready?"

Julia looked at the jacket, then at him. "Ask me about the arrows."

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: A getter that returns a reference to a private mutable object, such as a list, lets outside code change it, so programmers often return a copy instead.
story:
Sierra had been telling herself all week that the private keyword was basically a lock on a diary, and now the diary was empty and the lock was still on. She sat in the back row of the computer lab after last bell, headphones around her neck, staring at her screen where her Playlist class should have been holding four songs and was holding none.

"Run it again," said Zoey, pulling a chair over with a screech that made the only other person in the room, Jean, look up from his monitor like a meerkat.

"I've run it four times." Sierra tapped the test output. "See? Songs after setup: four. Songs after Jean's class runs: zero. My ArrayList is private. There's a getter. Nothing else touches it. So how."

Jean wandered over with the loose, innocent stroll of someone who absolutely knew something. "Maybe your computer is haunted. You should smudge it."

"You should be smudged," Sierra said. "Your ScreenSaver class ran right before the count went to zero. What did it do?"

"Nothing hedonistic," Jean said solemnly. "It was very restrained. It got the songs, admired them, gave them back."

Zoey leaned in, chewing the end of a pen, which was her peccadillo and everyone had learned to live with it. "Wait. Got them how? Show me the line."

Jean scrolled his own screen around with theatrical reluctance. There it was: a single line, getSongs().clear(), followed by a comment that just said "tidying."

"Tidying," Sierra repeated. "You tidied my private list."

"To be fair," Jean said, "you can't predicate your whole defense on the word private if you're handing people the list itself. That's like locking your diary and then mailing the diary to me."

Sierra opened her mouth to argue and then closed it, because that was annoyingly close to the thing she was starting to see. The field was private, sure. The getter didn't return the field's contents, it returned the field, the actual list, the actual object sitting in her class's memory, and a list you're holding is a list you can clear. Privacy in this language wasn't a wall. It was a wall with a dog door, and she had installed the dog door herself and labeled it getSongs.

"Okay," she said slowly. "So private protects the name, not the thing."

"Ooh," said Zoey. "Say that again but slower, I want to write it on my forearm."

Ms. Mercado came around the corner of the aisle with her mug, which everyone knew was tea and everyone pretended was coffee because she enjoyed the mystique. She looked at the three of them hovering over one keyboard, which in her class was usually a sign of either debugging or forgery. "Whose tragedy is this?"

"Mine," said Sierra. "My list got emptied by code from another class. Through my getter. Which I wrote. So it's also slightly mine in a different way."

Ms. Mercado sipped her tea and said nothing at all, which was her signature move, and Sierra understood it as permission to keep going rather than as help, because Ms. Mercado's whole philosophy was that if she explained things, nobody would remember them, but if you bled on the keyboard a little, you'd remember forever.

"So what do people do," Sierra said, mostly to the screen. "Never write getters? That can't be right, the assignment literally says getter methods."

Zoey spun the pen. "What if the getter doesn't hand back the real list? What if it hands back a copy? Like, you want to look at my songs, fine, here's a photocopy, go knock yourself out, clear it, fold it into a paper airplane, the original in my class doesn't care."

Sierra was already typing. She changed the return line, ran Jean's class again, and watched his tidy little clear() land harmlessly on the copy while her actual list sat there fat and intact with all four songs. She put both hands up like a goalkeeper who'd just saved a penalty.

Jean peered at her test output and frowned. "Huh. My tidy did nothing."

"It did something," Sierra said. "It tidied a photocopy. Very useful. Thank you for your service."

Then Zoey, who had gone uncharacteristically quiet, cleared her throat. "So, question. Hypothetically. If someone, not me, had written a CoffeeOrder class last night, and it got Zoey's, I mean its, list of orders through a getter from Jean's Barista class, and then that someone's code cleared it as a joke."

Jean's head turned very slowly. "When."

"Last night. Around eleven. And the Barista list may currently be empty and the Barista may currently believe the app is broken."

Sierra started laughing before she could decide whether to be sympathetic. "You did the exact same thing. You did the exact same thing to yourself, through your own getter."

"It was a different configuration of the same thing," Zoey said with dignity, already pulling up her files. "Fix mine next."

Jean slid his chair back to his own monitor, muttering, and Ms. Mercado drifted toward the door with her mug. Sierra copied her new return line, pasted it into Zoey's CoffeeOrder class, and hovered her finger over the run button.

"On three," Zoey said. "One, two."

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: The key signature of G major has one sharp, F-sharp, which applies to every F in the piece unless an accidental changes it.
story:
The music room smelled of floor polish and old radiators, and the upright piano against the wall had one key, the E below middle C, that stuck unless you hit it with conviction. Jake hit it with conviction now, four times, testing the opening of his sixteen-bar melody. It was due Friday. It was currently Wednesday, sixth period, and Ms. Kaya had already told him twice that "due Friday" did not mean "due Monday with a shrug."

"Play it again," said Arwa, who was sprawled on the riser steps with a bag of popcorn she had somehow smuggled past three hallway monitors. "The part you think is the good part."

"The good part is bars nine through twelve," Jake said, and played them, and stopped, and frowned.

Reid looked up from his phone. "Sounds like a doorbell apologizing."

"Your whole musical world is parochial," Jake said. "You think anything that isn't four chords and a haircut is pretentious."

"I think that's true, yes."

Jake played the bars again, slower. The tune was supposed to be in G major, bright, the kind of thing he'd worked out by humming on the bus until a woman gave him a seat out of pity. On the piano it had sounded right, yesterday, at home. On this piano, in manuscript, it had gone crooked somewhere around bar nine, sour in a way he couldn't put his finger on, like a word spelled correctly that still looked wrong.

"Wait," Arwa said, and came down off the risers, popcorn abandoned, which for Arwa was a serious commitment. "Play bar nine. Just bar nine." He played it. "Now play that F." He played the F. "And play the F you played yesterday at home."

Jake opened his mouth to demur, because he hadn't been at home yesterday, he'd been at his grandmother's, on her piano with the candlesticks and the photograph of nobody anybody could identify, and then he closed his mouth. At his grandmother's, he'd played F-sharp. He'd hummed it, felt it, leaned on it. Here, reading off his own manuscript paper, he'd written the F in bar nine as a plain, ordinary F, natural and innocent and completely wrong.

He looked at the top of his staff. One sharp, there at the beginning, where he'd carefully copied it from the board last week. F-sharp, sitting in the key signature like a little flag he'd forgotten he planted.

"The key signature," he said slowly. "It's not just for bar one."

"Congratulations," said Reid. "The音符 police will be notified."

"Don't do that," Jake said, but he was already flipping the pages of his manuscript, hunting F's. There were eleven of them. He'd written a sharp sign before the first one, in bar two, out of sheer anxiety, and none after that, because somewhere in his head the sharp belonged to that one F and that F alone, like a name tag. But the sharp at the beginning of the line applied to every F in the whole piece, all sixteen bars, unless you put an accidental in front of one to change it. The tune had known that. His ear had known that. Only his pencil hadn't.

"So yesterday you played it right," Arwa said, "and today you wrote it down wrong."

"The pencil betrayed me," Jake agreed.

"Play it right, then. From bar nine."

He played from bar nine with every F sharp, and the melody came back to itself, all the sourness gone, the doorbell suddenly confident about its news. Reid even lowered the phone, which was the closest thing to applause he issued. Ms. Kaya appeared in the doorway, drawn by either the music or the silence where the popcorn crunching had been, and listened with her head tilted.

"Better," she said. "Copy it out fresh before Friday. And Jake, the sharp at the beginning of your staff is doing more work than you think. Be kind to it."

"It's carrying the whole piece," Jake said. "It's the only one of us with a work ethic."

He found a blank sheet of staff paper and began copying, and this time he said each note name under his breath as he wrote, F-sharp, F-sharp, F-sharp, like a spell, like phonetics for a language where one letter had learned to lean.

"Why are you narrating?" Reid asked.

"Insurance," Jake said, and wrote bar nine.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Jeffrey Hall's 2018 study estimated that moving from casual friend to friend takes about 90 hours together.
story:
The house smelled like paint and cold air, and Nicholas stood in the middle of the living room holding his phone in one hand and a notebook in the other. The movers were not coming until morning. His mother had gone back to the old apartment to supervise the loading, which left him alone in a room with no furniture, no curtains, and a floor so new it still showed the pale rectangles where the builder had laid protective paper.

He had found the number three days ago, late at night, in an article his phone had surfaced for no reason he could determine. A researcher named Jeffrey Hall, in a 2018 study, had estimated that moving from casual friend to friend takes about 90 hours together. Ninety hours. Nicholas had read it twice, then opened his notebook and done the arithmetic in the dark. He and Elena had been in the same classes since seventh grade. He and Dani had ridden the same bus for four years. He had no idea, before that night, that friendship could be measured at all, and now he could not stop measuring it.

In the kitchen, where the echo was worst, he sat on the floor with his back against the cabinet and wrote out the hours. Cross country practice, two hours a day, five days a week, eleven weeks a season, three seasons with Dani running beside him. That alone was three hundred hours, and that was only the running. He felt something loosening in his chest, and he was honest enough with himself to admit it was relief. The numbers proved the friendships were real. But then he turned the notebook page and the relief soured, because he was moving to a town where he had zero hours with anyone, and ninety was a long way from zero.

He was still sitting there when he heard a car in the driveway. Dani had said she might come by after her shift, and she had said it in the flat voice she used when she was pretending not to care, the querulous tone of someone who has already decided to be annoyed at the world before the world does anything. She came in carrying a pizza box and looked around the empty room with her eyebrows raised. "You live like this now," she said. "Very minimalist."

They ate on the floor of the living room because there was nowhere else, and the pizza box between them was the only piece of furniture either of them owned in the whole town. Nicholas showed her the notebook. He explained it more carefully than he meant to, the way he did when a fact had taken hold of him, laying out the study the way his father laid out a hand of cards. Ninety hours, from a 2018 study, that was Jeffrey Hall's estimate, casual friend to friend. Dani listened with her chin on her knees.

"So what's the plan," she said. "You're going to clock in?"

"There's a running club at the new school. I emailed the coach. Practice starts the second week." He had done it that morning, before his mother was even awake, and he had not told anyone until now. "Two hours a day. If I go every day, that's the fastest way to stack hours with the same people. Same faces, every week, whether I like them yet or not."

"Whether you like them yet," Dani repeated. She pulled a slice loose and studied the cheese. "You're going to sit there and introspect about whether you like people, like it's a separate thing from knowing them."

"It is a separate thing. That's the whole point of the number. You can't shortcut it. You just have to show up and let the hours pile up, and somewhere in there it turns into something." He heard how it sounded even as he said it, like a recipe, like something you could follow. He wondered if that was the flaw in his thinking or the truth of it, and he let the question sit unanswered between them.

Dani set down her crust. The streetlight through the uncurtained window put a pale rectangle across the floorboards, the same size as the ones the paper had left, and she looked at it for a while. She had driven forty minutes to sit on the floor of an empty house with a boy who was doing math about her, and she found she could not decide whether that was insulting or the most Nicholas thing he had ever done. Probably both. She thought about the bus, four years of it, the slow accumulation of mornings she had never once counted, and she understood that he was trying to build a floor under himself before he fell, which was what he always did, and which she had always found endearing exactly until tonight.

"Here's what you're not accounting for," she said. "I know you. Three hundred hours of running, sure, but also the day I twisted my ankle at the meet and you walked me to the car while everyone else kept racing. That's not in your column anywhere. Your ninety hours gets you a friend, fine. It doesn't say anything about the rest."

Nicholas looked at the notebook, at the neat columns that had felt so solid an hour ago, and admitted to himself that she was right about the limits of it. The number was a floor, not a ceiling, and everything above the floor stayed unmeasured. He closed the notebook and set it on the pizza box.

Dani stayed until the streetlight went from white to amber and the room grew cold enough that they pulled their jackets across their shoulders. When she stood to leave, she paused at the door with her keys in her hand.

"Text me your practice schedule," she said. "I want to see the hours start."

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A violin's four strings are tuned in perfect fifths to G, D, A and E, from lowest to highest.
story:
Victor arrived at the community center early enough to hear the hallway still humming with the residue of the afternoon's basketball camp, sneakers and whistles echoing off the tile. Room 4 had been a storage closet before someone cleared out the folding chairs and hung a whiteboard. He unzipped the case on the table, and the violin inside caught the fluorescent light along its varnish. Four weeks of lessons, and his left hand still cramped after twenty minutes. He tuned by ear because the clip-on tuner was borrowed and Neveah had it today.

She came in with the tuner swinging from her backpack strap and dropped into the chair beside him. "I keep playing the wrong string," she said. "Mr. Balogun keeps saying lowest to highest and I nod like it means something."

"Which one do you grab when he says A?"

"The fat one." She plucked the lowest string and it thudded, dull as a rubber band.

"That's G." Victor laid his own violin flat on the table between them so the strings faced up like a map. "Look. From the low side, going up, it's G, then D, then A, then E. Each string sits a perfect fifth above the one before it." He plucked G, then D, and let the two sounds hang in the room together. "Hear how they're kin? That's the whole ladder."

Neveah leaned over the instrument, frowning. "So E is the skinny one at the top."

"The skinny one, the highest, yeah." He plucked A and then E so she could hear the same kinship repeated one rung up. "That's why the E string is the one that screams when you're sharp. Everything's stacked in the same gap, over and over."

Mr. Balogun appeared in the doorway with his coffee and watched them without coming in. "What's this, a lecture?"

"More like pragmatics," Victor said. "She needed the strings laid out where she could see them, not described."

"Fine," Mr. Balogun said. "As long as it holds." He tapped the doorframe twice and moved on toward the gym, and Neveah waited until his footsteps faded before she laughed, quiet, covering her mouth.

They ran the scale exercises together, and Victor noticed that explaining the ladder had settled something in his own head too. He had been treating the fingerboard as an axiom, a thing to accept without proof, when it was really an argument he could follow: string by string, fifth by fifth, up from G. For the first time he crossed from the D string to the A string without stopping to look at his hand.

The recital was in three weeks. Victor had signed his name on the sheet the day it went up, before his confidence had a chance to argue, and now the sign-up felt like a debt. His mother kept saying it would be good for his applications, which made him want to withdraw his name on principle. He historicized his own reluctance, tracing it backward: she had done the same thing with swimming, with chess club, with the coding bootcamp, each enthusiasm converted promptly into résumé language, and he had quit each one partly to spite the conversion and partly because he quit things. He could not tell which motive was load-bearing.

Neveah, for her part, watched Victor's fingers climb and thought about how he had looked laying the violin flat like a diagram, so certain of himself for once. She had assumed he was the kind of person who was simply good at things, the way she had assumed she was the kind who was not, and both assumptions were starting to look lazy. The tuner on her backpack strap had cost fourteen dollars and she had used it as a crutch, letting it tell her when she was close enough, never learning what close sounded like. He had never owned one. He tuned by fifths, leaning his ear against the grain of the strings.

"Play the G and the D again," she said. "Together."

He plucked them and let them ring. "Hear it?"

"It's the same sound as A and E. Just lower."

"That's the trick of the whole instrument."

She picked up her own violin, laid her fingers where the ladder told her they belonged, and drew the bow across the A string, then up to the E, clean, no squeal. Her eyes went wide. "Do that again," she said, mostly to herself, and did.

The door opened and Mr. Balogun leaned in. "Recital order is posted," he said. "Victor, you're after the piano girl. Neveah, you want a slot?"

Neveah looked at her violin, then at Victor, who said nothing, who was carefully not deciding for her. "Put me down," she said.

"Two weeks of practice between you and public humiliation," Mr. Balogun said. "Use them." He wrote something on his clipboard and left.

Neveah set her bow down and rolled her shoulders. "You're going to play, though. Actually play?"

"That's the rumor." Victor picked up his violin and set his fingers on the D string, ready to climb to the A. "Count me in."

"From G?" she asked, and he nodded, and they both drew their bows across the lowest string at the same moment, the doubled note filling the little room and rolling out into the hallway behind it.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Canada's first food bank opened in Edmonton on January 16, 1981.
story:
The notice had said the food bank ran out of the common room at Fairview Seniors' Residence on the second Saturday of the month, and Clara had assumed that meant the residents organized it. It turned out they were partly the clients. She learned this at nine in the morning, standing beside a folding table stacked with tins, while a woman named Mrs. Okafor pinned numbers to a corkboard and explained that residents on fixed incomes could shop after the public had been served.

Reuben was already there, wearing the same orange lanyard she'd been handed, sorting pasta by shape with the seriousness of someone who had done this before. "You didn't know either," he said, reading her face. "It's fine. I didn't know food banks were even that old a thing here. I looked it up last night because my mom asked. Canada's first one opened in Edmonton, January 16, 1981." He held up a box of macaroni as if presenting evidence. "Nineteen eighty-one. That's younger than my parents."

Clara took the box from him and shelved it. She had signed up because her scholarship application wanted community service, which she suspected was a corrupted motive, and because she genuinely believed hunger was wrong, which felt cleaner. She had not expected the two feelings to sit so close together, or to be so hard to tell apart. She was still deciding what to do about that when Mr. Romano arrived.

He came with his own wheeled cart, and he did not take a number. He was small and neat and moved like a man who had spent decades being precise about things. "I want the labels facing out," he told her, "and I'll choose my own groceries. I've eaten for eighty-one years. I know what I eat." Mrs. Okafor explained, gently, that the standard practice was pre-made hampers, for fairness and speed. Mr. Romano said, "Fairness," the way you'd repeat a word in a language you suspected of lying to you, and parked his cart where it would obstruct the most traffic.

While Mrs. Okafor was pulled away by a delivery, Clara stood at the table with him. He asked her, not unkindly, whether she thought it was profligate of him to reject a hamper that might contain food he wouldn't use, letting good tins go to waste out of pride. She said she didn't think pride was waste. He looked at her for a moment, then said that in his day, if a man wanted a revolution, he became a dissident and printed pamphlets; now apparently you brought a shopping cart to a church basement and insisted on choosing your own soup. It was almost a joke. Almost.

She let him choose. She walked the table with him and turned labels out as he pointed, and when he took an extra jar of tomato sauce beyond the posted limit, she logged it as a substitution rather than an addition, a small act of bookkeeping she wasn't sure exonerated her from anything but did keep Mrs. Okafor from having to argue with an eighty-one-year-old man over pasta. Reuben watched from the sorting corner and gave her a look she chose to interpret as solidarity.

Later, during the lull before the residents' hour, she found Mr. Romano by the window with his coffee. "1981," she said. "Food banks here. Does that seem late to you, or early?" He turned his cup slowly. "I was forty-three," he said. "I remember when there weren't any, and I remember nobody saying we needed any, and then suddenly we needed them everywhere. You can decide for yourself what happened in between." He did not offer more, and she found she liked that he didn't.

Clara filled out her hours sheet at the sign-in table and left the line about what she had learned blank, then wrote, deleted, and wrote again: that helping wasn't one thing, that dignity and efficiency pulled against each other, that a system forty-some years old was both an accomplishment and an accusation, and that she could hold all of that at once without resolving it. Reuben snapped his lanyard off beside her. "Same shift next month?" he asked. She looked over at Mr. Romano's cart, packed the way he wanted it, labels out. "Same shift," she said, and pulled the door open into the cold.

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: Herman and Chomsky's second filter is advertising: outlets that depend on advertisers' money have a reason to avoid coverage that drives those advertisers away.
story:
The printer at school had been broken all week, so Emma carried the twenty proof pages of the Corridor Review to the coffee shop on Miller Street, spread them across the corner table, and began reading with a red pen in her teeth. She was sixteen and the news editor, a title she had wanted for a year and now found heavier than expected. The lead story was hers: the district had hired a contractor to renovate the football field, the contractor had missed two deadlines, and the field was still fenced mud in November. She had interviewed three players, a groundskeeper, and a school board member who had asked, twice, to be quoted carefully.

Jessica slid into the opposite chair with a hot chocolate and a reputation for reading over people's shoulders. "Is that the field story? Annabelle says the contractor's son is in her chemistry class. She says nobody's mad about the fences. They're mad you wrote it."

"Someone has to," Emma said, and heard how flat it came out, like a line from a movie about someone braver.

Jessica pulled one page toward her. "It's good. It's careful. You dichotomize everything, though. Board versus students, them versus us. Maybe the board just picked badly. Maybe the contractor is overwhelmed."

"That's not the story I have sources for."

"Then say that somewhere. Say what you don't know." Jessica licked chocolate off her thumb and pointed at the back page, where the ads lived. "You should look at this part too."

The back page was mostly one ad. Hartley's Sporting Goods, green and gold, had bought a quarter page every month for two years, and that money paid for the printer that was currently broken. Emma looked at the ad, then at her headline, and then, because she did not want to look at either again, out the window at the wet sidewalk.

Mr. Francis came in at four, the way he did every Thursday, ordered a black coffee, and stopped at her table because the pages were impossible not to notice. He was the paper's faculty advisor, a reticent man who signed the budget forms and mostly let the students fail on their own. He read the field story standing up, all the way through, without touching his cup.

"Solid sourcing," he said. "Well paced."

"Then what's wrong with your face?"

"Nothing's wrong with my face." He sat down anyway. "Hartley's called the front office this morning. The owner's cousin is on the school board. He said he'd pull the ads if this runs."

Emma felt the pen in her hand go still. "Can he do that?"

"He can. It's his money." Mr. Francis turned his coffee cup a quarter turn, then another. "In my media studies course we read Herman and Chomsky. Their second filter is advertising. Outlets that depend on advertisers' money have a reason to avoid coverage that drives those advertisers away." He said it plainly, like reading a definition off a card, and then he sat back. "That's not me telling you what to print. That's me telling you what you're standing in."

"So we soften it. Cut the board member's quote, say the timeline 'faced challenges.'" Emma heard herself and hated it. "That's what you're saying, right? That's the practical thing."

"I'm saying Hartley's pays for your printer."

Jessica, who had been quiet in a way Jessica was rarely quiet, said, "Print it. Find new ads. Bake sales."

"The printer costs more than bake sales," Emma said. "You know that."

But even as she argued, she was working through it, and she did not like where she arrived. She thought about the city paper, the one her mother read, and how it ran full-page spreads for the hospital whose expansion it covered in six warm paragraphs. She had always assumed that was a coincidence of tone. Now she could not stop seeing the shape underneath, the way money made a groove and coverage rolled along inside it. At the same time, Mr. Francis had not told her to kill the story, and the school board member had answered her questions, and the world was not a single machine grinding everyone into the same paste. Both things seemed true at once, and she lacked the talent to dichotomize them cleanly, which Jessica would probably call a compliment.

"I'm not softening the field story," Emma said finally. "But I'm cutting the sentence about the cousin. That's not sourced, it's just a thing Annabelle heard. And I'm writing a note to Hartley's, asking whether they want to respond for the next issue, on the record."

"That's a strange half-measure," Mr. Francis said.

"It's not a half-measure. It's the measure I can actually defend." She began gathering the pages, squaring them against the table edge. "We might lose the ad. We might not. I don't know yet, and I'm not going to pretend I do."

"You're going to be an impossible editor," he said, but he was almost smiling into his cup.

He carried his coffee toward the window seat, and Jessica reached across and steadied the stack of pages before it could slide. Behind the counter, the girl at the register was taping a flyer to the register glass, a flyer printed, Emma noticed, with a Hartley's logo in the corner. Jessica saw it at the same moment.

"Emma," she said. "Look."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: A Hanukkah menorah has nine branches: eight for the nights of the holiday and one for the shamash, the helper candle used to light the others, one more each night.
story:
Blake's mother had cajoled him into coming to the community Hanukkah party at the cultural center by promising there would be people his age, which turned out to mean Nolan and Selena, both of whom he knew from AP Chem and neither of whom he would have chosen for a Saturday. The gym smelled of frying latkes and floor wax, and a long table near the stage held three menorahs of different sizes, the tallest almost two feet, its branches polished to a dull gold.

"Your family's doing the lighting," his mother said, pinching his sleeve. "Fourth night. Go find the rabbi's table and get the candles."

The box of candles was thinner than he expected. He counted out what he thought he needed, walked to the tall menorah, and stopped. Eight arms branched outward in a curve, and a ninth stood higher than the rest, apart. He had never paid attention before. His grandfather used to light it at home while Blake played games under the table, and the detail had never once surfaced.

He set four candles in the holders, then doubted himself. Was it four, because it was the fourth night? He glanced at the other menorahs. One had three candles waiting; the other had five, already lit, and a family was singing around it in a language he half knew. Somewhere between four and five, the count had slipped his mind. He stood there with two candles in his fist, sweating in his coat.

Selena appeared beside him, holding a paper plate of sufganiyot, powdered sugar dust on her sleeve. "Are you stuck?"

"No," he said, and then, because she kept looking, "Sort of. How many does the menorah even take? I lost the night."

"The nine-branch thing?" She nodded at the holders. "Eight for the nights, plus the tall one in the middle. That's the shamash, the helper. You use it to light the others, one more each night."

So the one he'd been ignoring his whole childhood had a job. He lifted the fourth candle back out of the holder he'd miscounted into, rearranged, and set the shamash last. "Why can't you just light them with a match?"

"Beats me. Ask Mr. Mwangi."

Mr. Mwangi, who taught world history at the high school and apparently came to everything at the cultural center, was at the latke table arguing gently with a volunteer about whether the potato pancake could rightly be called autochthonous to anybody's cuisine, since potatoes had crossed an ocean twice before anyone fried them in oil. "The latke is a migrant," he was saying, "and proud of it." He caught Blake's expression and raised an eyebrow.

Blake didn't ask him anything. He was tired of adults supplying answers at parties. Instead he stood at the menorah with the shamash candle unlit, watching a man from the choir hold a lit taper from the five-candle menorah, because apparently you could borrow fire from one to another, and thought about his grandfather. His grandfather had been a pragmatist about most things, the thermostat, the car, the news, but never about this, never about the candles, and Blake had assumed that was just old-man sentiment. Now it seemed more like the opposite: the helper candle existed precisely because somebody, a long time ago, had wanted the holy ones to stay holy and put the work on a separate shoulder.

He lit the shamash from the borrowed taper. The flame leaned in the draft from the heating vents. His mother was already filming on her phone, and Nolan had drifted over with his own plate, and the room was loud with the hiss of the fryers and forty conversations.

"You going to do it or just commune with it?" Nolan said, mouth full.

Blake touched the shamash to the four waiting candles, one, two, three, four, and recited the blessing his mother mouthed at him across the crowd, getting most of the syllables. Then, out of some impulse he didn't examine, he used the shamash to relight a candle on the neighboring menorah that a toddler had blown out while nobody was watching.

"That one wasn't ours," Selena said.

"I know," Blake said, and held the helper candle up, its flame still burning, still taller than all the rest.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: The Situation-Behavior-Impact model, from the Center for Creative Leadership, frames feedback by naming when it happened, what the person did, and what effect it had.
story:
Ajay's kitchen smelled like burnt popcorn and ambition, which was roughly what their robotics team ran on. Kevin sat at the counter while Ajay paced, holding the scrimmage results like a subpoena. They had lost by four points, and the loss traced back to one moment: Chelsea, their driver, had frozen during the endgame and missed the climb, and afterward Ajay had told her, in front of everyone, that she had "choked like a fountain pen." She had left the garage with her headphones already on.

"You can't just say that to her," Kevin said. "You said it in front of the whole team. She'll quit."

"She should introspect a little, honestly." Ajay dropped into the chair across from him. "If I froze at regionals, I'd want someone to tell me."

"You would want someone to insult you?"

Ajay opened his mouth, then closed it, which for Ajay was practically a written apology. Kevin pulled out his phone, where he'd saved a page from a leadership handbook Ms. Reddy had left on the classroom shelf, mostly as a joke, back when he'd been looking for a book about knots. He read it twice before he understood why it had snagged him. "There's this thing called the Situation-Behavior-Impact model," he said. "From the Center for Creative Leadership. You name the situation, the behavior, and the impact."

"Sounds like a tax form."

"It kind of is. Like indemnity paperwork. Box one, box two, box three." Kevin scrolled. "Instead of 'you're lazy,' you say, like, in Thursday's meeting, which is the situation, you missed the deadline for the arm code, that's the behavior, and we lost the build day, that's the impact."

Ajay squinted at the screen as though it might be penurious with its wisdom, offering less than it owed. "So no verdicts. Just receipts."

"Just receipts."

They practiced on each other, which was where it got fun. Kevin tried the model on Ajay's popcorn technique. "Situation: Tuesday night. Behavior: you set the microwave to four minutes. Impact: the kitchen smells like a small arson event." Ajay laughed so hard he knocked over his water, and while they mopped it with the last clean dish towel, he tried one back. "Situation: every practice since September. Behavior: you narrate your own driving like a golf announcer. Impact: Chelsea mimics you in the girls' bathroom, and she's good at it."

"I do not narrate."

"'Kevin approaches the rings with confidence,'" Ajay said, in a low commentator's rumble, "'though his history with the left ring suggests caution.'" Kevin threw a popcorn kernel at him, one of the unburnt ones, because it was true and they both knew it. That was the strange part, he thought, stacking the kernels into a small ziggurat. The model wasn't about being nicer. It was about being exact. You could still say the hard thing, but you had to aim it, the way you aimed the robot at the rings, instead of spraying it across the whole garage and hitting Chelsea in the face.

The next morning Chelsea was in the school parking lot before first bell, sitting on the tailgate of her mom's truck and pretending to read a manual she was holding upside down. Kevin walked over, felt his stomach do the little drop it did before a climb, and started anyway.

"Saturday, endgame," he said. "You didn't call the climb, and the signal was there for about three seconds. And we lost the match by four, so we missed finals by one ranking point." He heard how it sounded, clean and small, no verdict anywhere in it. "That's it. That's all I wanted to say."

Chelsea turned the manual right side up. "Ajay sent me a text at one in the morning that just said 'my bad, fountain pen thing, that was out of line.' Which, for Ajay, is basically indemnity." She studied Kevin for a second. "You practiced this on someone, didn't you."

"We may have run several simulations."

"I want to hear the one about the golf announcer."

"That information is classified," Kevin said. Chelsea laughed, the actual kind, and hopped down off the tailgate, and shoved the manual into her bag. "Fine. But Saturday I'm calling the climb early, and if you narrate it, I'm driving us into the wall."

"Kevin sets up for the climb," he began, already rumbling, and she shoved him toward the doors while the first bell rang.

activity: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
knowledge_domain: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
fact: In 1942 sociologist Robert K. Merton named 'organized skepticism' as a norm of science: claims must survive critical scrutiny by the community before they are accepted.
story:
I am not a sloppy person. I titrated each sample three times, or close to three, and my averages were consistent, which is more than anyone could say about Mario's poster with its crooked glue sticks. So when the judges at regionals kept asking who else had run my numbers, I thought they were just looking for reasons to knock me down. Johanna said maybe they weren't. Johanna says things like that, quietly, as if she were sorry for them.

Mr. Jung arranged the museum trip for the whole senior class, some unit on how knowledge gets made, and I went because missing class is missing class. The place smelled like floor wax and old stone, the kind of cold that gets into your wrists. Johanna drifted toward the Impressionists. I wanted the hall of scientific instruments, brass balances and glass phials under dim glass, because I figured that was my territory. Mario followed me, eating something he'd smuggled in, which tells you about Mario.

The middle of the hall was given over to how science actually works, or claims to, with big pale panels of text. I read them out of spite, honestly, hunting for ammunition. There was a panel about a study on stomach ulcers that nobody believed for years, and one about cold fusion, which sounded like a vacation package but was apparently two chemists announcing something that fell apart when other laboratories tried it and got nothing. A tour guide was telling a group of middle schoolers, "One experiment convinces nobody. Do you know how many times this result was repeated? Teams all over the world, for years." The kids looked like they wanted lunch.

Then I found the panel with the name. In 1942, the sociologist Robert K. Merton had set out the norms of science, and one of them he called organized skepticism, the requirement that claims survive critical scrutiny by the community before being accepted. I stood there long enough that Mario came and read over my shoulder, still chewing. "In 1942?" he said. "Sociologist Robert K. Merton called it organized skepticism. Huh." He said it like he was quoting a cereal box, but I felt something shift, an inchoate irritation whose shape I hadn't let myself see. The judges weren't accusing me. They were doing the job the whole system was built around.

"You're taking their side now," I said, which was a stupid thing to say to a wall panel, but I said it to Mario anyway.

"I'm reading a wall," Mario said. "You're the one arguing with it."

Johanna found us there, sketching the brass balances in a little notebook she keeps. She asked what the panel said, and I told her, all of it, the year and the name and the norm, and she was quiet in that way of hers. "I could run your titrations," she said finally. "My mom has the kit in the garage. If I get your numbers, they're your numbers. If I don't, they're nobody's." That seemed fair and also terrifying, which should have told me something right there.

We did it that Sunday in her garage, the same orange juice, the same indicator, the light coming gray through the little window over the workbench. She worked slowly and I watched, correcting her grip on the burette twice even though her grip was fine. Her first result came in high. Her second came in high again. Not wildly, but enough. I sat on an upturned bucket and thought about the third run of my own titrations, the one I had cut short the day of regionals because the bus was coming and the first two agreed anyway and I wanted lunch. I had told myself, and then told everyone, three times. Close to three. There is a difference, it turns out, and the difference is the whole story.

Johanna let me do the third one myself while she watched, and it landed between mine and hers, in the gap where the truth probably lived. I said we should run it again, and she said she had to be home by six. On the drive back, Mario talked the entire way about his economics homework, stagflation, prices rising while everything stalls, and I barely heard him, because I was composing the email to the judges in my head. I wrote it that night, honest, the short version: my result did not replicate cleanly, further trials pending. It cost me the state finalist slot. The coach of another team called our school to say, of all things, that it was the most professional retraction he'd seen from a student, and my mother framed the email as if it were an award.

Here is the part I keep turning over. The week after I sent it, Mr. Jung stopped me in the hallway to say the regional director had forwarded it to the program committee as a model of good practice, and they wanted me to speak on a panel next spring. The very scrutiny I'd resented had become the thing with my name on it, which felt less like winning than like being handed the bill and told it was a gift. I said I'd think about it. That afternoon, Johanna and I went back to the museum on our own, and we stood in front of Merton's panel for a while, saying nothing. A docent was telling a tour group, "Science isn't a list of answers. It's a list of things that haven't been disproven yet." A kid near the front raised his hand and asked, "So how do we know anything's true?" "We don't," the docant said cheerfully. "We just keep asking." Johanna wrote that down in her little notebook, and then she looked at me and said, "You're smiling."

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: The secret printed ballot is called the Australian ballot because Australian colonies, Tasmania and Victoria, introduced it in 1856.
story:
The ballot came on a Tuesday, in an envelope Jake nearly threw out with the pizza menus. He carried it up to his room and set it on the desk beside his half-finished geography essay about the isthmus of Panama, that narrow bridge of land that connected two continents and divided two oceans, which seemed to him now like a metaphor for something, though he couldn't say what. He had three days to fill it out and drop it at the collection box outside the library, and his mother had already asked twice whether he'd done it, in the voice she used for dentist appointments.

He hadn't done it because he couldn't decide about the school board race. For governor and for the measures he knew his answers; those had come to him quickly, almost embarrassingly so, the way he'd internalized his parents' positions over eighteen years of dinner-table arguments without ever examining them. But the school board had six candidates for two seats, and one of them, Ms. Alvarez, had taught him sophomore English and been the first adult to tell him he could write. Another, whose name he kept forgetting, was running on a promise to change the way the district handled security, which a lot of parents at his little brother's school wanted. Jake had read both of their statements four times and each time found himself agreeing with about sixty percent of each.

Mahi came over Thursday evening, ostensibly to study for the calculus final, actually to lie on Jake's floor and talk about anything else. She spotted the envelope immediately.

"You haven't sent it," she said. It wasn't a question.

"I'm deciding."

"Between Alvarez and the other guy, I know, you've texted me the whole saga." She sat up, cross-legged. "Just vote Alvarez. She's the one you actually know."

"That's kind of the problem," Jake said. "I know her. So I know I like her. But liking someone isn't the same as agreeing with them, and I think I might actually agree with the other guy more, on the stuff that matters."

"Then vote for the other guy."

"Then I'm voting against the teacher who told me I could write. Which feels like a betrayal, which I know is a stupid feeling, but it doesn't stop being a feeling just because I know it's stupid." He heard how it sounded as he said it, circular and overdramatic, and he kept going anyway because it was true.

Mahi picked at the carpet. In her nonchalant way, eyes elsewhere, she said, "At least nobody has to know which one you pick."

"Except me," Jake said. "I have to know."

He walked her out at nine, and on the way back through the kitchen his mother was at the table with her own ballot, marked and sealed, waiting for morning. He stood there for a minute watching her read the back of a cereal box like it was urgent. She had voted in every election since she was twenty-one, he suddenly understood, dozens of these small sealed envelopes, and he had never once seen her mark one. He asked her why it was all so private, why you couldn't even show someone if you wanted to, and she said she didn't make the rules, and he went upstairs feeling like the question was still sitting on the counter.

He looked it up. It took four searches to get past the noise, and then there it was, plainly stated: the secret printed ballot was called the Australian ballot, because the Australian colonies, Tasmania and Victoria, introduced it in 1856. He read the sentence twice, then a third time. It had a name. Somebody, somewhere, had invented this thing he'd assumed was just how voting fell out of the sky, and it had traveled from those colonies to his desk in a suburb where his father had been born. He sat with that for a while. The secrecy wasn't a rule someone handed down to him; it was a designed thing, chosen, and people had fought about it before he existed.

Calder texted him at eleven: did you vote yet or are you still being a philosopher about the school board. Jake typed three replies and deleted them. The secret ballot meant that whatever he marked, no one could ever audit his conscience about it, not Mahi, not his mother, not the candidates themselves. The whole design trusted him to hold both loyalties, the personal one and the reasoned one, in the dark, alone. That was either mercy or burden, and he suspected it was both, and that nobody could tell him which.

In the morning he sat at the desk with a black pen and the Panama essay still open beside him. He filled in governor. He filled in the measures. Then he held the pen over the school board race for a long moment, and he filled in one oval, one only, and folded the paper so even he couldn't see it anymore, and sealed the envelope, and pressed along the flap with his thumb.

He dropped it through the slot of the library box on his way to school. Mahi was waiting by the doors.

"So?" she said.

"Voted," Jake said, and walked inside.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: US employers withhold 6.2 percent of an employee's wages for Social Security tax, up to a yearly wage limit.
story:
Justine had done the arithmetic twice on the back of her ticket-roll sheet before the lobby lights came up for intermission. Eighteen hours at eleven dollars an hour was one hundred ninety-eight dollars. The number on the check the manager had handed her in a thin envelope was smaller, and she wanted to know where the difference had gone before she spent any of it.

She waited until the concessions stand went quiet, then unfolded the pay stub on the counter beside the popcorn machine. There were lines she recognized, like the hourly wages, and lines she did not, each with its own subtraction. Gregory was restocking the napkin dispensers, and he had opinions about most things, so she called him over.

"I worked eighteen hours," she said. "This isn't eighteen times eleven."

Gregory wiped his hands on his apron and leaned in. He had worked at the theater since the previous spring, saving for a car he described to anyone who would listen as his putative freedom machine, a silver hatchback he had not yet test driven. "Look at the FICA line," he said. "Everybody yells about it their first check."

"Social Security," Justine read aloud. The stub showed a percentage next to it. She took the pen from behind the napkin dispenser and did the division in the margin. Six point two percent of her wages, taken out, matched the missing amount exactly, to the cent. "So it comes off every check."

"Up to a point," Gregory said. "There's a limit. Once your wages for the year go over it, they stop taking that part. You'd have to earn a lot more than we do here for that to matter."

Justine wrote the yearly limit on the corner of the sheet and looked at it. She had been planning the money already, in her head, on the walk to work: a portion for the deposit on the dorm microfridge she and her roommate would split, a portion for the bus pass, a portion unscheduled. The arithmetic in her head had been simple, and the actual arithmetic was simple too, once she saw it, but it was a different simple.

Kashton came through the lobby with a broom and interposed himself between them and the doorway where Ms. Chukwu was doing the evening count in the box office. "She's in a mood," he said quietly. "Someone put the wrong film on screen three and forty people wanted refunds."

Justine folded the stub and put it in her apron pocket. Later, during the last showing, she sat in the projection corridor with the disbursement schedule the manager had pinned to the corkboard, the calendar that told them which Friday the checks would appear. She recalculated the microfridge, the bus pass, the unscheduled portion. Six point two percent off the top, every check, until the year's wages passed a limit she would not reach at eleven dollars an hour. It was not a scam and it was not a mystery. It was a rule she now knew, and knowing it changed the plan without ruining it, which was, she was starting to suspect, how most rules worked.

She was still uncertain about one thing, and she said so to Gregory when he came up to thread the reel. "I can't decide if it's fair," she said. "I did the hours. They took the money before it ever reached me."

"Fair or not, it's coming out either way," Gregory said. He held the film up to the corridor light and squinted at the sprocket holes. "Meanwhile I'm two hundred short on the hatchback, and Ms. Chukwu won't give me the Sunday closing shift because you asked for it first."

Justine looked at the schedule clipped beside the disbursement calendar, her name in the Sunday box, his name crossed out. She had wanted that shift the way she had wanted the whole job, cleanly, without thinking about who else had wanted it. She thought about six point two percent, taken off the top before anyone got to decide, and about a car that was still only putative, and about how little these two facts had to do with each other, and how she was going to have to decide something anyway.

"Take the Sunday close," she said. "I'll take your Saturday matinees. It's the same hours."

Gregory threaded the reel and started the motor. "You're sure?"

The projector lamp came up and the screen downstairs flickered white, then blue, then filled with the opening credits of the last show of the night. "Roll it," Justine said.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: The SAT switched to a digital, adaptive format in the United States in March 2024: how well a student does on the first module of each section sets the difficulty of the second.
story:
The cursor blinked in the password field for the third time before Jake typed it correctly. The applicant portal loaded slowly, the way it always did on his mother's old laptop, and there it was at the top of the page: your application is complete and under review. Nothing else. No date, no hint. He sat back in the kitchen chair and pressed his palms against his eyes.

He had submitted the application eleven days ago, and in that time he had checked the portal nineteen times, a number he knew because he had counted, and which he had told no one. The uncertainty had begun to transmute into something almost physical, a tightness behind his ribs that showed up in the middle of geometry homework, at dinner, once in the shower. His scores were already in the file. That was the part he kept circling back to, because the scores had felt like a coin toss at the time.

Jaime found him still sitting there when she came over to return his calculus notes. She pulled out the other chair and watched the screen over his shoulder. "Still nothing?"

"Still nothing," Jake said. "And I can't stop thinking about the math section."

"You got a decent score."

"I got a score I can't explain." He turned the laptop toward her. "The second module was brutal. Harder than anything I'd practiced. I walked out convinced I'd bombed it. Then the score comes back higher than any of my practice tests. Higher than the one I actually understood."
