Jaime laughed, a short, surprised sound. "You don't know how it works?"

"Enlighten me."

"It's adaptive," she said. "The SAT switched to the digital, adaptive format in March of 2024, in the United States. How well you do on the first module of each section sets the difficulty of the second."

Jake stared at her. "Sets it how?"

"Better first module, harder second module." She shrugged, as if it were obvious, and for her it was; her older sister had prepped a year after the change. "So the brutal questions weren't the bad news. They might have been the good news."

"That's it," Jake said quietly. He leaned back and looked at the ceiling, where a water stain from two winters ago had spread into the shape of a small country. "I spent a month thinking I got lucky. That the score was some clerical fluke and the college would see through it."

"Or you earned it, and the test knew before you did."

He turned that over. He wanted to accept it cleanly, the way Jaime had offered it, but something in him resisted. If the harder module meant he had done well, then the score was real. But he still couldn't shake the memory of sitting in that testing room, certain he was failing, hands cold on the keyboard. His own judgment had been that wrong. So which should he trust now, sitting in judgment over his whole application, his essay, his chances? The evidence, or the feeling?

The back door opened and Mr. Gupta from next door came in with a plate of his wife's samosas, which he left whenever he suspected Jake's mother was working the night shift again, which she was. He set the plate between them, pithy as ever: "Eating well, both of you." Then he was gone, and Jaime took a samosa and pointed at the screen.

"Refresh it."

"It's been four hours."

"Refresh it anyway. For me."

He refreshed it. The page reloaded with the same words, the same blank blue banner, and Jake closed the laptop lid halfway, then thought better of it and closed it all the way. There was a small rapprochement happening inside him, between the boy who had panicked in the testing room and the one who apparently had earned the harder questions, and it did not need the portal's permission to continue.

"Do you want to go get food?" Jaime asked, already standing, already gathering her bag. "Real food. Not samosas."

"We have samosas."

"Jake. Food. Outside. Now."

He slid the laptop to the far end of the counter, where he wouldn't be able to see it glow if anyone messaged, and grabbed his jacket off the hook. At the door he paused, went back, and turned the laptop so it faced the wall.

"That's not going to change anything," Jaime said from the doorway.

"I know," Jake said. "Let's go."

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: A footnote appears at the bottom of the page where the reference occurs, while an endnote collects the same kind of note at the end of the paper or chapter.
story:
Avery spread the printout across the kitchen table at ten past nine on a Sunday night, with the paper due Monday morning. The document looked right until page eleven, where every one of her notes had collected itself into a block at the end, numbered and orderly and completely in the wrong place. She had spent two weeks on the argument, three days on the sources, and now the formatting had rearranged itself behind her back.

"Endnotes," Hanna said from the other side of the table, leaning over her own chemistry flashcards. "That happened to me in October."

"What's the difference?" Avery asked. She was half-afraid the answer would be nothing, that she had worried over a distinction that didn't exist.

Hanna tapped page three, where a small superscript number floated at the end of Avery's sentence about textile mills. "A footnote appears at the bottom of the page where the reference occurs," she said. "An endnote collects the same kind of note at the end of the paper or chapter. So you've got endnotes. Whether that's allowed depends on Mr. Wiśniewski."

Avery looked at the clock. Eleven hours until the deadline, and the answer to whether she had to fix this would decide how she spent ten of them.

She remembered, then, the first week of the semester, when Mr. Wiśniewski had stood at the whiteboard and said that a research paper was not a report. A report told you what happened; an argument told you what it meant. He had drawn a line down the board. On the left he wrote sources, on the right he wrote you, and he said the paper lived in the space between, in the place where evidence got bent into a position. Avery had thought at the time that he was being abstract for the sake of it. She thought so less now, at the kitchen table, with her own argument about child labor laws in front of her, because she had discovered the bending was harder than the finding.

Chaya had sent her the article at eleven that morning, a scanned chapter arguing that the factory acts had expropriated the earnings of the very children they claimed to protect, since the children had been pulled from wages into schools their families could not otherwise afford. Avery had built her third section around it, and then had spent an hour staring at her own paragraph because it had started to sound tautological: the laws protected children because they were protective laws. She had cut two sentences and written a better one, about how the parliamentary debate used the word protection for both wages and schooling, which let the politicians claim the same moral ground while the actual ground shifted underneath.

Chaya texted back within a minute when Avery asked about the notes. "Wiśniewski said footnote style, but he also said the point of citation is that a reader can follow you. Ask him?" Avery texted Mr. Wiśniewski, then remembered it was Sunday night, then texted anyway. While she waited she opened the settings in the word processor and found the option, sitting under the insert menu where it had been all along, and the notes migrated down to the bottom of each page as she watched, small numbers settling at the foot of the page where each reference occurred. Page three now carried its own note at its own bottom edge. It looked like the papers in the textbook example, like the model he had handed out.

The reply came at nine-forty. "Either is honest, but the assignment said footnotes. Fix it if it's quick." It had taken her ninety seconds. She sat back and looked at the clock, at all the hours she had just been given back, and then at her third section, where the sentence about parliamentary language still bothered her. She had evidence that the word protection was used two ways, but she did not have evidence that this was deliberate rather than sloppy, and she knew it.

She left the sentence in. She underlined it in pencil on the printout and wrote in the margin, might be me overreaching, and decided she would say so if he asked. Chaya had once told her that a syllogism was only as good as its first claim, and that most bad essays went wrong at the beginning, not the end, and Avery had filed it away as something to use someday. She was using it now. Her first claim was that the same word could carry two economies, and she was not certain of it.

She printed the final version at ten-thirty. Hanna gathered her flashcards and stood in the doorway with her coat half on. "Show me the footnotes," Hanna said, so Avery turned to page three and held it out.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: ISO 216 paper sizes such as A4 have sides in the ratio of 1 to the square root of 2, so cutting a sheet in half gives two sheets of the same shape.
story:
Jonathan had the kitchen table to himself until five, which gave him, by his arithmetic, two hours to finish a poster for Elle's river cleanup fundraiser before his mother came home and reclaimed the surface for dinner. The poster was a collage of cut paper, a riparian scene: herons in gray, reeds in green, a wide blue band of river that he had been trying to titrate toward turquoise, sheet by sheet, without ever landing on the right color. The library printer only did A4, and Elle wanted a big A3 version for the community board at the pool, so he was cutting and layering at the small size and hoping the enlargement would not ruin his proportions.

Everett arrived at four with a bag of chips and no intention of helping. He sat down across from Jonathan, ate, and offered commentary. "The heron looks like it's being arrested," he said. "It does not." "Wings up like that? It's being told to put its hands where I can see them." Jonathan adjusted the wings anyway, which he knew was a concession, and Everett grinned and stole a strip of blue paper to make a paper airplane out of his hat brim, which failed, which pleased them both.

The real problem arrived when Jonathan laid his cut sheets against each other and understood that he had built the design in pieces, not as one image. To enlarge it at the library, he would have to scale each piece separately, and he had no idea how to keep the relationships between the pieces intact. If he blew up the heron by one amount and the reeds by another, the whole scene would come apart, the heron looming over the reeds like a kaiju. He told Everett this, and Everett, chewing, said, "So just don't blow it up. Tell Elle small is the new big." "Everett." "I'm a ideas person, not a execution person."

Elle came in through the back door at half past four, hair wet from the pool, and went straight for the chips. This is where things stopped being simple, at least for her. Elle had spent the afternoon arguing with the lifeguard about whether the fundraiser poster should show the river as it actually looked, murky and half-choked, or as they wanted it to look, clean and blue and full of herons that were not technically herons but were technically aspirational. She had argued for the aspirational version, and she had won, and she was not entirely sure she deserved to win. Now here was Jonathan's poster, all clean water and graceful birds, and she found she wanted to poke a hole in it, or in herself, she couldn't tell which.

"That blue's too pretty," she said. Jonathan looked up, wounded. "It's two hours of my life." "I know. That's the problem." She sat down at the table next to him and pulled the bag of chips out of Everett's reach, out of principle. "The river's brown right now. Mostly brown. If people think it's already beautiful, why clean it?" "Because herons," Everett said, through chips. "Because herons," Jonathan agreed, and then, because he wanted to win the point, "Also, sit down and look at this, because I need a witness." He took a fresh A4 sheet, folded it in half, and cut along the fold. He laid the two halves one above the other, then set the full sheet beside them. "Same shape," he said. "Every single time. A4, you cut it in half, you get two sheets the exact same shape as the one you started with."

Elle picked up the halves and turned them, skeptical, the way she was skeptical about everything now, apparently. "That can't be true for any size." "It's the ratio," Jonathan said, hunting through his backpack for the sheet Mr. Foster had handed out in design class, a diagram he had shoved in a folder and forgotten. He found it and smoothed it flat on the table. "One to the square root of two. ISO 216, that's the standard, and that's why it works: because the sides are in that ratio, cutting a sheet in half gives two sheets of the same shape." She looked at the diagram, then at the paper in her hands, then, briefly, at Jonathan, and he watched her expression do something he'd only ever seen it do during debate rounds, when an argument she'd dismissed turned out to be load-bearing. "So if I print my pieces on A4, and scale every one to A3," he said, "the shapes match up exactly. Everything blows up together. The heron stays the right size to be arrested by the reeds." "Kaiju-free," Everett confirmed.

They went to the library at six with the pieces in a folder and the folder under Jonathan's arm like something valuable. At the printer he asked the cashier for A3, and the cashier, who had seen every kind of paper disaster and had opinions about all of them, loaded the tray and said, "Design in A4?" "A4," Jonathan said. The machine hummed. The first enlarged sheet came out and Elle snatched it before it had finished cooling, laid the smaller original in the corner, and traced the edges with one finger. Line for line, the shapes matched, the big heron exactly the big version of the small heron, and she laughed, once, loudly enough that a man at the computers looked over.

"So the river," Jonathan said, feeding the next sheet in. Elle was still holding the first one, tilted toward the window light. "It can be blue in the poster," she said. "Brown in the grant application, blue in the poster. Two papers, same shape." Everett said that was the most terrifying sentence she'd ever produced, and she threw a crumpled chip bag at him, and Jonathan pressed print.

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: The SIFT method from educator Mike Caulfield stands for Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, and Trace claims to their original context.
story:
The video arrived at 9:47 on a Tuesday morning, while Anais was still at her grandmother's table with the last of the toast. It showed a street turned into a river, a man clinging to a stop sign, brown water dragging a car sideways past a pharmacy. The caption said it was the flood two towns over, happening now, and the group chat was already lit up. Eva had written, "omg is this real," and Haroon had written, "sharing this, people need to see it before they drive anywhere."

Anais's thumb hovered over the forward arrow. Her grandmother, who did not own a smartphone and did not believe in them, was at the sink rinsing the same glass she had rinsed twice already, a small ritual of her days now that she forgot which things had been done. Anais had come for the week because her mother thought the house needed watching, and it did: the bills on the hall table, the kettle left on. She felt an atavistic pull toward the forward arrow too, the old instinct to be the one who warns the tribe, to be first with the fire.

She stopped, though, because of something Ms. Rajapakse had said on the last day of the school year, almost in passing, while collecting the shared laptops. She had mentioned a man named Mike Caulfield, an educator, and a thing he called the SIFT method, which stood for Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, and Trace claims to their original context. Anais had written it in the margin of her planner and forgotten it. Now she dug the planner out of her backpack, the spiral binding catching on her sweater, and read her own cramped pencil: SIFT. Stop was first. She put the phone face down on the table and finished her toast, which felt absurd and also, somehow, like the whole point.

Then she investigated the source. The account that posted the video had a username made of numbers and a profile picture of a sunset. It had existed for eleven days. It followed four thousand people and was followed by nine. She sat with that for a minute, her grandmother humming something at the sink, half a song from a decade Anais had never lived in.

Finding better coverage meant looking for someone else reporting the same thing. She opened the local paper's site, then the regional one, then the county emergency alerts. There was a flood watch, yes, but the river was three feet below flood stage, and the photos from the actual town showed a wet parking lot and some teenagers splash biking. No river-street, no stop sign, no car being carried off like a toy.

The last step was the one that felt like detective work, the one she would never have thought of on her own. She took a screenshot of a frame and ran a reverse image search on it, holding her breath while the little wheel spun. The same video had been posted four years earlier, after a hurricane in a different state, on a news station's page, where it was labeled correctly and timestamped. Someone had cropped the station's logo out. The clipping was neat, almost professional, which unsettled her more than anything else, the care of it.

She typed all this into the chat, then deleted it because it sounded like she was about to pontificate, and she could already see Haroon's face, the way he rolled his eyes when people lectured. Instead she sent the link to the original broadcast and wrote, "it's from 2021, different state. found it with a reverse image search." Eva replied with a single exclamation mark. Haroon replied an hour later: "good catch. I already sent it to my mom though." Then, "she cancelled her dentist appointment."

Anais put the phone down and went to find her grandmother, who was standing in the hallway holding the rinsed glass, looking at the hall table as if it belonged to strangers. Anais took the glass, steered her gently toward the living room, and sat with her while the old woman explained, in no particular order, how the well on this property had been dug before the town water came, how it drew from the aquifer that ran under three counties, how her late husband had never trusted anything that came out of a pipe he couldn't see the source of. "You always want to know where the water's been," her grandmother said, tapping the arm of the chair. Anais laughed, then felt something catch in her throat, and didn't say why.

She never found out who had re-posted the video, or why, and she knew she couldn't prove the flood watch hadn't been worth worrying about; the river could still rise. That part stayed uncertain, and she was honest with herself about it, in the dark of the guest room, phone glowing on her chest. But the next morning, when a new video came through, a warehouse fire this time, captioned with the word "NOW," she watched Haroon's name appear in the typing bubble, then stop, then start again, then stop. A minute later he posted only a link to the fire department's page, and nothing else, and Eva sent a small thumbs up. Anais screenshotted the exchange, for no reason she could defend, and her grandmother called from the kitchen, "Anais, the kettle," and she went.

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: The Soviet Union refused Marshall Plan aid and pressed Eastern European governments, including Czechoslovakia, to withdraw after first showing interest.
story:
The essay was due on Thursday, and by Monday afternoon Justin had filled two pages of his notebook with arrows that pointed at each other. Ms. Koné had assigned them a task that seemed, at first, almost kind: read two historians on the origins of the Cold War, then decide which account the evidence better supported. One historian argued that the United States had overreacted, treating every Soviet gesture as aggression. The other argued that the Soviet Union had closed itself off deliberately, that the division of Europe was chosen, not inevitable. The kindness ended there, because Justin could not find a fact that both writers had not already bent to fit their argument.

He had claimed the table by the window in the school library, the one with the wobbly leg that everyone else avoided, and spread his books across it like evidence at a trial. Margaret found him there after fifth period, carrying a paper cup of vending machine hot chocolate that smelled faintly of cardboard.

"You look like you're losing," she said.

"I'm cross-examining a dead Austrian man and losing."

She sat down anyway, which was either loyalty or boredom, and pulled the nearest book toward her. "What's this map?" It was a reproduced poster from the era, a map of Europe with the countries receiving American economic aid shaded in gray. The western half of the continent was a solid block of it. East of a certain line, the map went blank.

"They got money," Justin said, pointing west. "They didn't." His finger stopped on Czechoslovakia, an unshaded gap between the shaded zones, and something about its position bothered him. He flipped back to the index of the second historian's book, then forward to a page he'd dog-eared and un-dog-eared twice already. When he found the paragraph, he read it three times before he trusted it.

"Listen to this," he said. "The Soviet Union refused Marshall Plan aid. And it pressed the Eastern European governments to withdraw, too. Including Czechoslovakia, which had shown interest at first. Actual interest. And then pulled out." He sat back. "So that's why the map is blank there. It's not that nobody asked."

Margaret leaned over the map again. "So the second guy wins? Case closed, can we get snacks?"

"That's what I thought for about ninety seconds." He pulled the first historian's book back across the table. "But this guy says the Americans designed the plan so the Soviets would refuse it. That the terms were meant to be unacceptable." He tapped the page. "He doesn't say the refusal didn't happen. He says it was wanted."

"So both of them can use the same fact?"

"Both of them do use the same fact. That's the horrible part."

Margaret drank her cardboard hot chocolate and offered him the marshmallow sludge at the bottom, which he declined on principle. Before she left for track practice, she made him promise to stop making the arrow diagram, because she said it looked like a conspiracy board, and conspiracy boards were how reasonable people became Wikipedia editors.

That night, Justin did something he'd been avoiding: he messaged Meghan, who had already written her essay and had the infuriating habit of finishing things early. He composed the note at his kitchen table while his mother washed dishes behind him.

"Okay," he typed. "I give up on finding a fact that settles it. Question: when you wrote yours, did you pick a side?" He added, "Be honest. I can tell when you're being diplomatic because you use too many commas."

Her reply came while he was brushing his teeth. "I picked a side, but then Ms. Koné wrote 'good, now what can't you decide' on my draft in red pen, so maybe that's the actual assignment. Also my little brother used your yearbook photo as a coaster. You're welcome."

He stood in the hallway holding his phone and reread the red-pen sentence until it stopped sounding like criticism and started sounding like permission.

On Wednesday he wrote the essay straight through, and it was stranger and quieter than anything he'd drafted before. The Soviet refusal, he argued, was real, and Czechoslovakia's initial interest was real, and any account that treated the blank half of the map as proof of pure Soviet aggression was leaving out the possibility that the invitation itself had been shaped with the refusal in mind. But any account that treated the refusal as pure American theater, he also argued, was doing the same thing in reverse: assuming that because one side benefited from a choice, the other side never truly made it. He could weigh the explanations against the map, and the map favored the second historian more than the first. It did not, however, convict him outright. What stayed uncertain was intention, which no map could shade in gray.

When Ms. Koné handed the essays back on Friday, her comments on most papers were brisk, a word or two. On his she had written something longer, and he read it walking out through the library, past his wobbly table, which someone else had claimed with a calculus textbook and a look of settled despair. The comment was, for her, effusive: "This is the only paper that admitted what it couldn't know and still took a position. Come tell me why you left out the Austrian's argument about Germany. I have opinions."

Justin stood by the window where the light came through onto the carpet in long afternoon bars. He had left it out because the paragraph had refused to behave, and now he would have to defend the omission out loud, without arrows, without a diagram, in a room with a teacher who had opinions. He folded the paper in half, put it in his back pocket, and walked toward her classroom door, which was still open.

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
knowledge_domain: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
fact: A coda is an optional closing section after the recapitulation that reinforces the home key and brings the movement to an end.
story:
The deadline was Sunday night, because Ms. Jung collected the marked scores on Monday morning, and Madeline had left her grandmother's house the only quiet place she knew with only the weekend to finish. The photocopied first movement of Mozart's Piano Sonata in A major lay on the dining table beside a cup of tea her grandmother had brought without being asked, and Madeline had three coloured pencils and a page of instructions that said: mark the exposition, the development, the recapitulation.

She had done this before with Trinity, on a Haydn movement, and they had argued the whole way through. Trinity marked by instinct, by where the music seemed to change its mind, while Madeline marked by rule: the exposition ended at the double bar, the development ended when the first theme came back in the home key. Two systems that mostly agreed but not always, which was the thing that had kept Madeline awake on Tuesday, the idea that structure could be both a fact and a feeling. Ms. Jung had said only, "Both of you will defend your markings in class," as if that enfranchised the disagreement itself, gave it standing in the room.

Now, alone, she worked pencil-first. Exposition in blue, brackets around the first theme, the second theme, the closing section, the double bar. Development in green: Mozart took a fragment of the closing theme and pushed it through keys the way her grandmother pushed a threaded needle through linen, patient, sideways, nowhere she expected. Then the recapitulation began, and Madeline switched to red, and marked the first theme's return, the second theme, now restored to the home key, everything folding back like a map along its old creases.

Then her red pencil stopped and the music did not.

There were still four lines of score left. Bars of pure A major, chords stacking up, the same cadence repeated as if the movement could not let go of saying goodbye. Her instructions said nothing about this. She checked her green and blue and red brackets three times, and they were right, she was nearly certain they were right, and the music kept going anyway, beyond everything she had been taught to name.

She texted Trinity. "My markings run out before the music does. Did that happen to you?" The reply came as a photo of Trinity's score, same problem, same orphaned bars, and beneath it: "idk. Odin says it's part of the recap. But it doesn't have the themes in it." Madeline looked again. It was true, there was no theme, only cadence, only arrival, the home key stated and restated until it stopped.

Her grandmother came through with the tea tray and paused at the table. "Is that Mozart?" she said. She had played, decades ago, badly by her own account and with great pleasure, and Madeline had always suspected the pleasure had been the more hedonistic than the discipline was strict. "Play it for me. I can't read the markings."

There was an old upright in the front room, its top holding a framed photograph of a man Madeline had never met. She played the exposition, clumsy, then the development, then the recapitulation, and then the last bars, the ones she could not label, and her grandmother, standing at the window with her hands folded, said, "That's the coda." Madeline kept her hands on the keys. "It's a closing section after the recapitulation," her grandmother went on, "when he wants one. It's optional. It just reinforces the home key and brings the movement to its end." She said it the way she said things about linen, matter-of-fact, from long use. "Not every movement has one. That's why your teacher didn't put it in the instructions, I expect."

Madeline copied the word into the margin in red, coda, with a bracket, then sat looking at it. It was a small thing, four lines of score, a word she could have found in the textbook if she had read past the assigned pages, but it had already begun to feel like the Haydn argument again: the rules ended and the music continued, and the music itself had a word for its own continuation, which meant somebody, sometime, had needed that word badly enough to make it. Whether structure was a fact or a feeling, or a fact with room left over, she still could not say, and Monday was coming either way. She texted Trinity one line: "It's called a coda. It's optional." Then she lifted the lid of the piano and played the last four bars again, alone, all A major, until the sound stopped ringing in the frame of the old house.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Acrylic paint is water-based while wet, but it dries quickly and becomes water-resistant once dry.
story:
Madison had claimed the table by the window in the public library at four o'clock, which meant she had another ninety minutes before the after-school crowd swallowed it. Spread before her lay a half-finished painting for the county youth art show, a wide scene of the harbor in her town with the ferry coming in through fog she had mixed from three grays. She had brought her own brushes, the good ones, the sable ones her grandmother had given her, because the library's community art cart held nothing but plastic brushes with the consistency of disappointed celery.

Her friends had plans of their own. Laetitia was one table over with a stack of AP Bio flashcards, and Mitchell had come ostensibly to study for the driving test but was mostly reading a comic hidden inside the driver's manual, a machination so transparent that even the librarian had stopped pretending not to notice. Madison waved them over to look at the ferry.

"It needs something," she said. "The water's too flat."

"It's beautiful," Laetitia said, in the tone of someone trying to be supportive of a decision she privately considered wrong. "It looks like a postcard."

"That's the problem. Postcards are dead." Madison leaned close to the canvas, hunting for what was missing, and decided the answer was texture, chop, something alive in the harbor. She thinned a dish of acrylic with water from her bottle, working the brush until the paint ran loose and obedient. Acrylic was strange that way, she thought, bending to water while it was wet, and she had learned to keep it damp or it betrayed her.

The trouble was that the reference photo of the ferry was in her backpack, in the car, four blocks away. Mitchell had driven them, and he had the keys.

"I beseech you," she said, holding out her hand.

"We just got here."

"Four blocks. Two minutes."

Mitchell sighed the sigh of the deeply put-upon and dug in his pocket. Laetitia came with her, leaving her flashcards fanned on the table like a hand of cards, and the two of them went out into the October air. They found the photo, bought three cookies at the bakery because it seemed criminal to pass it, argued about whether Laetitia's grandmother was actually rude or just French, and walked back. It took twenty-five minutes. Madison was telling a story with her hands when she pushed through the library door, and she stopped mid-gesture.

Her brushes lay across the dish of paint, exactly where she had dropped them, bristles down. The clock above the returns desk confirmed what her stomach already knew. She sat, lifted the largest brush, and it came up rigid as a tiny club, its point hardened into a bent claw. She carried them to the sink in the corner and ran warm water over them, working the bristles with her fingers, but the paint had set into something that no longer cared about water at all. It was Laetitia who said it, watching over her shoulder: "It's water-based while it's wet, isn't it. But once it's dry, it's water-resistant. It's like the paint changes teams." Madison kept scrubbing. The second brush had gone stiff at an angle, a permanent crook, and the third, the small one she used for rigging and gull-wings, held its dried skin of blue like a husk.

She returned to the table peevish, which was unfair, and she knew it was unfair, and she was peevish anyway. She snapped open her case and laid the ruined three in a row. Sixteen dollars each, the art store guy had said. Her grandmother had said they would outlast her if she cared for them, and she had promised she would, and now she had broken the promise for a photograph she hadn't even needed, because she knew the ferry by heart.

But she still had twenty minutes of good light, and the harbor still needed chop. She picked up the crooked brush, the one bent at that permanent angle, and dragged it sideways across the waterline. The stiff, half-clogged bristles skipped and scratched, leaving broken streaks, gaps, a stuttering line of white over the gray. She tried it again farther along. It looked like light on water. It looked, honestly, better than anything the good brushes had done all afternoon, and she worked up the whole harbor with the ruined tools while Mitchell held the cookie bag out of range of the splatter and Laetitia turned her flashcards face down to watch.

By closing time the painting was done, and done well, and Madison was carrying it flat across her arms toward the door when Mitchell, reaching to hold the door for her with elaborate courtesy, knocked his water bottle off the table. It hit the floor, cap first, and sent up a jet of water that caught the corner of the canvas and pooled across the harbor. Madison froze. Mitchell made a strangled noise of apology. Laetitia lunged with a sleeve.

The water sat on the surface, beading, glittering under the lights, and lifted nothing with it. Madison tilted the canvas and watched it run off in a clean sheet, the ferry and the fog and the scratched white chop all exactly where she had left them. She looked at the ruined brush in her hand, still bent, still stubborn, and started to laugh.

"Two cookies," she said, holding out her palm to Mitchell. "And you're driving me to the art store."

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: The United States baby boom generation was born between 1946 and 1964, and its bulge on the pyramid has now moved into the retirement ages.
story:
Noemie had claimed the corner table by the periodicals an hour before closing, and the population pyramid of the United States still refused to tell her anything. Mr. Sok had assigned it plainly enough: analyze the chart, then predict whether the country would need more schools or more nursing homes, and defend the prediction in a paragraph. The chart itself was a orange-and-blue barbell, wide at the middle, narrow at the top, and she had copied its shape twice into her notebook as though familiarity might turn into understanding.

Across from her, Jaxen was studying for a chemistry test, his flashcards fanned out like a losing hand of cards. "Allotropes," he said, tapping a card. "Different forms of the same element. Diamond and graphite, both just carbon." He said it with the mild wonder of someone who found the fact personally comforting, and Noemie wrote it down in her margin without thinking, because it felt true of something she couldn't name yet.

Aurelie arrived with two hot chocolates and zero patience for the pyramid. "It's a histogram turned on its side," she said, sliding a cup across. "Old people, young people, count the bars, write the paragraph, come to the game with me." She leaned over Noemie's shoulder and began to expatiate on the injustice of homework assigned on a Friday, a speech Noemie had heard in shorter and longer versions all year, and this one threatened to be prolix enough to consume the remaining hour of library time.

"That's the point, though," Noemie said. "It's not just counting." She tapped the thick middle section where the bars swelled outward on both sides. "If the bulge is young, you build schools. If the bulge is old, you build nursing homes. The whole answer is where this part sits, and I can't tell what it means." She said it and then stopped, because something in her own sentence had snagged. The bulge. She knew a bulge. She had grown up inside one.

Her grandmother volunteered at the library on Friday afternoons, reshelving returns in the large-print section, and Noemie had watched her push the cart past the periodicals twice already without waving her over. Now she raised her hand, and her grandmother came and stood at the table with a stack of mysteries balanced against her hip. Noemie pulled her toward the chart. "Grandma. What year were you born?"

"1951, sweetheart. You've asked me that for some project or other every year since fourth grade."

"And Grandpa?"

"1949." Her grandmother squinted at the pyramid, then at Noemie's finger resting on the widest band of bars, the ones that reached furthest out from the center. Noemie ran her finger along the age labels beside the bars until she found the ages that matched people born in 1949 and 1951, and the bars were thick, and above them the chart thinned toward nothing, and below them it thinned too before widening again slightly near the bottom. She said the words out loud, half to herself. "They're the bulge."

Aurelie frowned. "What bulge?"

"The baby boom," Noemie said. "Everyone born between 1946 and 1964. My grandparents, both of them. All those people at once, and now look where the bulge is." She traced it upward with her pen, to where the thick bars sat in the oldest section of the chart, the retirement ages at the very top. Her grandmother watched her do it and said, "That's why the line at the pharmacy is so long, dear," and went back to her cart, and the three of them watched her go.

Noemie began to write, then stopped. "But here's what I can't decide," she said. "The bottom of the pyramid isn't empty. There are still kids. So it's not only nursing homes. It's both, and the question wants one answer." Jaxen looked up from his flashcards, and she looked back at the margin where she'd written allotrope, at the same country holding two shapes at once. "Maybe the honest answer is that the ratio shifts. More of one, but the other never goes to zero." She wrote the paragraph anyway, hedging in the middle of it, and underlined the years 1946 and 1964 twice.

Aurelie stole a sip of her hot chocolate and checked the time. "Library closes in ten minutes. Are you coming to the game or are you staying to argue with a bar chart?" Noemie packed her bag slowly, notebook last so the page with the underlined years lay flat against her chemistry notes, her grandmother's years, and zipped it shut. "Coming," she said. "But I'm stopping at the pharmacy first, to see if Grandma needs a ride home."

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: A video cannot be reverse-searched directly by most image engines, so fact-checkers take screenshots of key frames and search those images instead.
story:
The video arrived at 11:42 on a Tuesday night, while Sydney was sitting on her grandmother's screened porch watching moths throw themselves against the wire. Melina had sent it to their group chat with the message THIS IS TONIGHT, and the clip showed a flooded street, brown water to the car doors, a man on a roof waving a white shirt. Melbourne floods LIVE, said the caption. Twenty thousand shares already. Sydney's thumb hovered over the forward arrow.

"Send it to the neighborhood list," her grandmother said from the doorway, drying her hands on a dish towel. "Choi's on that list. He'll want to know before the roads go." Her grandmother valorized that kind of speed, being first with news, and Sydney had grown up hearing about the value of a fast tongue. But she'd also spent the spring in Mr. Choi's media seminar, where he'd made them spend a whole class on a single question: where did this come from? She could still hear him say it, tapping the projector screen. Not what is it. Where is it from.

She typed a reply to Melina, then deleted it. Then typed again. "Checking first," she sent, which earned back three eye-roll emojis from Cassandra, whose ebullient certainty about everything had only increased since graduation. Sydney put the phone face-down on the porch table, and the cicadas filled the silence with their dry, engine sound.

Her grandmother's laptop sat inside on the kitchen table, propped open to a crossword. Sydney brought it out to the porch and tried what seemed obvious: pasting the video's link into an image search. Nothing useful came back, just the same clip on other feeds, the same caption copied forward like a chain letter. She tried pasting the video itself. The search engine sat there, blank and indifferent, refusing the file the way a vending machine refuses a crumpled bill. Whatever everyone claimed about looking things up, a video was not a picture, and the tools she knew were built for pictures.

She was about to give the whole thing up as Melina's problem when she remembered something Mr. Choi had mentioned offhand, half a joke at the end of class: "Fact-checkers screenshot the frames. You can't reverse-search the video itself with most of these engines, so you take screenshots of the key frames and search those instead." He'd waved his hand like it was nothing, a trick of the trade. She paused the clip where the floodwater touched the car door handles, screenshotted it, and dropped the still image into the reverse image search.

The results loaded slowly on the porch, the wifi being what it was at the edge of the county. Sydney sat with her hands folded, not refreshing, making herself wait. When the page finally assembled itself, the first result was not from Melbourne and not from tonight. It was from two years ago, a regional newspaper, a town she'd never heard of, the same man on the same roof in the same white shirt. The second result was the same photo again, older still, from an agency's archive. The clip had been recaptioned and relaunched, a ghost pulled out of storage and dressed in tonight's date.

Her stomach did something cold and slow. She scrolled further. Melina had already sent it to her cousin, who ran a community page with four thousand followers. Sydney's own grandmother was standing at the sink now, saying something about checking on the Hendersons' culvert, taking it for granted that the flood was real because the girl on the porch had all the erudition of the young and would surely know.

"Grandma." Sydney carried the laptop inside and set it on the counter beside the dish rack. "That video's old. It's not from tonight. I checked the frames." She showed her the side-by-side, the identical shirt, the identical water line, the dates stacked under each image. Her grandmother squinted, then touched the screen with one finger as though the glass might argue.

"So it's a lie," her grandmother said.

"It's a real flood," Sydney said. "Just not this one." She found she couldn't make it simpler than that. Somewhere between the two statements was the truth she hadn't figured out how to hold yet: that people were passing it on out of genuine worry, that the worry was for a real place, and that the clip was still false, still capable of sending four thousand people out to sandbag a street that had never been wet.

She texted Melina the screenshots. Melina replied a minute later with "wait what," then "omg I sent it to Priya's page," then a longer pause. Cassandra wrote that it didn't really matter since floods like that happen all the time, and Sydney started to type the obvious reply and stopped, because she wasn't sure how much it mattered either. A false video about a true kind of disaster. She sat with that, the phone warm in her hand, the kitchen clock loud.

Outside, headlights swept the driveway and a car door closed. Mr. Choi came up the walk carrying a casserole dish, returning the pan from the funeral lunch, and Sydney went out to meet him holding the laptop open, the two images glowing side by side. "Before you look at the neighborhood list," she said. "Look at this first."

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: The Taylor rule, proposed by economist John Taylor, says that when inflation rises one percentage point a central bank should raise its interest rate by more than one percentage point.
story:
The hardware store on Delmore Street opened at seven, but Xavier arrived at six-thirty because Ms. Chen, the owner, had told him the till needed counting before the first contractor came through the door. He was eighteen, three weeks out of high school, and this was his first job that involved a key. The key was heavy, brass, older than he was, and it turned with a sound like a small animal clearing its throat. Behind him, the street was still blue with early light, and a garbage truck fermenting its summer load idled at the corner, filling the air with a sweet rot he could taste at the back of his tongue.

Xavier had taken the job for money, but he kept it, he admitted to himself on slow afternoons, for the conversations. Ms. Chen had run the store for twenty-six years and believed that every customer who walked in was a problem to be solved rather than a transaction to be completed. She had a dry, unhurried way of talking that made even a dispute over a refund feel like a chess game played in another room. She also had opinions about the economy, and the economy, that August, was doing things that gave her plenty to say.

The trouble started with Tegan, who worked the afternoon shift and was, like Xavier, heading to college in September. Tegan had been in the economics club at their school and had strong convictions delivered at high speed. On Tuesday, between selling a crate of screws and arguing with the ladder inventory on the computer, Tegan leaned on the counter and declared that the central bank was overreacting. "Inflation goes up one point," Tegan said, tapping the countertop for emphasis, "they raise rates by like two. It's punitive. Just match it. One for one. Inflation up one, rate up one, done. Anything more is just hurting people with mortgages for no reason."

Xavier said nothing at first, because he didn't actually know. He had signed up for an economics elective in the fall, mostly because Yuna had described the professor as "a legend," and until that moment he had assumed the whole subject was graphs and obviousness. But Tegan's confidence had a suspicious brightness to it, the kind Xavier recognized from his own worst moments in debate class, and it made him want to check.

He checked that evening on his phone, sitting on the floor of the break room while the store's ancient radio muttered a moribund weather forecast about a heat wave that had already ended. The search led him to something called the Taylor rule, proposed by an economist named John Taylor. He read the sentence twice, then a third time, because it seemed at first too simple to be the answer. When inflation rises one percentage point, the central bank should raise its interest rate by more than one percentage point. Not equal to it. More than it. He sat with that for a while, turning a leftover price sticker over in his fingers, feeling the odd pleasure of a small fact rearranging a large opinion. He didn't fully understand why the rule said more, and the honest part of him noted that and set it aside, like a part left over after assembling a shelf.

The next afternoon Tegan was back on the subject before Xavier had his apron on. "You thought about it?" Tegan asked. "One for one. Tell me I'm wrong."

"You're wrong," Xavier said, and held up a hand before Tegan could accelerate. "The Taylor rule. John Taylor. When inflation rises one percentage point, the central bank raises its rate by more than one percentage point. More, not the same."

Tegan blinked. "That's a rule? With a name?"

"That's what it's called," Xavier said. He had rehearsed the line on the bus, partly for accuracy and partly so he wouldn't say "like" in the middle of it.

Ms. Chen, restocking near the window, made a small sound that was almost a laugh. "The boy reads," she said, to no one in particular.

Tegan was quiet for a moment, which was rare enough that Xavier marked it. "Okay," Tegan said slowly, "but I still think people are getting squeezed. So the rule says more than one, and I think that hurts. Both things can be true, right?"

That was the question Xavier took home with him, along with the smell of sawdust that never fully came out of his clothes. He thought about it while restocking, while sweeping, while explaining to a customer why the cheaper caulk was a form of parasitism on your own future walls, an image he'd stolen from Ms. Chen and delivered, he thought, with some style. He thought about it on the walk to the bus stop, past the shuttered bakery whose windows still displayed a faded cake someone had never collected.

On Friday, Yuna came in for picture hooks and stayed twenty minutes leaning against the display of levels, which Tegan pointed out was thematically appropriate. The three of them argued in low voices over the beeping of the scanner, Yuna taking Tegan's side out of loyalty to the underdog, Xavier holding his narrow ground. He said the rule existed for a reason, and that people smarter than him had thought about it, and that Tegan's point about squeezed borrowers was also real, and that he didn't yet know how both of those fit together. Tegan called that a cop-out. Yuna called it honest. Ms. Chen rang up a hammer in the middle of it all and said, "Three college students and no customers. This is what the interest rate has come to."

Xavier laughed, then turned the fact over once more in his mind, the way he'd been doing all week, like a stone with one side he still hadn't seen. The bell over the door chimed, and he went to see what the customer needed.

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: The derivative of a constant is zero, so adding 7 to a function shifts its graph up but leaves its derivative unchanged.
story:
Mr. Diallo had taped the problem to the whiteboard before anyone arrived, and it was still there when Hailey came in with her bag half unzipped, the way it had been all week, the way things were when her mother's hours at the clinic got cut and the house went quiet with arithmetic of its own. The problem asked for the maximum of a function that described, of all things, the height of a kicked ball, and Hailey had promised herself she would understand it before the regional meet, because Maya was counting on her for the calculus round and Maya was already carrying too much.

She sat down across from Jessie, who had claimed the good table by the window, and pulled out her notes. Mr. Diallo had taught them the rule last week: bring the exponent down, subtract one. She could do it on a polynomial with her eyes almost closed. The problem was the next part, finding where the graph peaked, where the derivative went to zero and the function turned around and started falling.

Maya arrived late, hair damp from the rain, and dropped into the chair beside her. "Okay," Maya said, "I got the derivative, but I think I messed up the original function, because Jessie has a different one and we got the same answer for the maximum, which means one of us copied wrong."

Jessie turned her notebook around. Her function ended in a plus seven. Maya's ended in a plus two.

"You dropped a five somewhere," Jessie said.

"I didn't drop anything. Check the setup." Maya's voice had an edge, the kind that came from wanting to be right and being tired, both at once. Hailey knew the sound. She had made it herself at the dinner table two nights ago, defending her decision to keep the math club even though the bus fare was eating what little her mother called the entertainment budget, a penurious category that had lately come to mean everything that wasn't rent or groceries.

Hailey took both notebooks. She differentiated Maya's function first, dragging the exponent down, subtracting one, and then she did Jessie's. She looked at the two results for a long moment.

"They're the same," she said. "Both derivatives. Exactly the same."

"That's impossible," Jessie said. "Different functions, different derivatives."

"Then I made the mistake," Maya said, "because two people can't both be right with different answers, that's not how this works."

Hailey didn't answer right away. She drew both graphs quickly, roughly, side by side. Maya's curve, then Jessie's curve. Then she slid her pencil under Maya's graph and lifted it, mentally, straight up until the two curves sat one on top of the other, separated by exactly the distance between a two and a seven.

"Watch," she said, and she said it slowly, because she was building it as she spoke. "The derivative of a constant is zero. So adding seven to a function shifts its graph up but leaves its derivative unchanged." She tapped the two drawings. "Yours is Jessie's, pushed up. Five up. Same slope everywhere, same peak in the same place, just higher."

The room went quiet in the way it did when something landed. Maya leaned over the graphs, then back, then over again, as if distance would change what she saw.

"So neither of us made the mistake," Maya said.

"Neither of you. You instantiated the same problem two ways." Hailey was proud of that sentence, maybe too proud, and she let it stand anyway.

Mr. Diallo had drifted over from the calculators, arms folded, listening without correcting, which was his way. He looked at the graphs and raised his eyebrows at Hailey, a small permission. She took a breath and finished the actual problem on the board, setting the shared derivative equal to zero, solving for the point where the ball stopped climbing, then feeding it back into the function to get the maximum height. Two different maximum heights, actually. Maya's and Jessie's. Both correct, five units apart.

"Genotype and phenotype," Jessie said suddenly, tapping the pencil against her chin. "Like in bio. Same genes, same instructions, different height depending on the environment."

"That is not what those words mean," Maya said.

"It's close to what they mean."

"It's not."

"It's adjacent."

Hailey laughed, and it came out easier than she expected. She copied the graphs into her notes, drew the little arrow showing the lift of five, and wrote underneath it, in small letters, the fact she had found. She was aware, as she wrote, that she hadn't explained why the constant vanished when she differentiated, only that it did. Somewhere under the surface there was a reason, a mechanism, a thing Mr. Diallo would show them next week or the week after, and she would have to be patient with the gap between knowing that something was true and knowing why. For now it was enough that it worked, that the maximum sat where the derivative said it would, every time she checked.

Maya nudged her elbow. "Regional meet. You're doing the calculus round."

"I'm doing the calculus round," Hailey said. She zipped her bag all the way, for once, and slung it over her shoulder. Outside, the rain had stopped, and the parking lot shone under the lights.

"How are you getting home?" Maya asked.

"Bus. It's fine."

"Jessie's mom's here," Maya said. "We'll drop you."

Hailey stood in the doorway a second, notes against her chest, the two lifted graphs still visible in her mind like a thing balanced on a fingertip. Then she followed them out.

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: False friends are words that look alike in two languages but differ in meaning; Spanish 'embarazada' means pregnant, not embarrassed.
story:
The folding table in Wilson's garage still had the ring from a paint can someone had never wiped, and Charlotte set her index cards on it like they were dishes she was afraid to break. Across from her, Adrienne peeled an orange in one long spiral, which she could do and Charlotte could not, and which seemed, at the moment, like one more way Adrienne was better prepared for the world.

"Five minutes," Adrienne said, "all in Spanish, on whether the voting age should drop to sixteen. Then I take the other side." She pulled the spiral of peel apart and laid it flat. "Ms. Buchanan does this to everyone in the exchange program. She says the point is to think in the language before you translate."

Charlotte had written her opening in English first and moved it over word by word, which she already suspected was cheating in some way she couldn't name. She knew the vocabulary. She could conjugate the subjunctive in her sleep. But when she tried to hold an argument in Spanish, the sentences kept sliding out from under her, like furniture on a slick floor.

"Empecemos," Adrienne said, and started the timer on her phone.

Charlotte began with the cards, then abandoned them. "Los jóvenes de dieciséis años pagan impuestos," she said, sixteen-year-olds pay taxes, "y trabajan, y conducen coches." She was three sentences in and starting to feel the argument gather weight when she reached for the word for embarrassed. She wanted to say that politicians should be embarrassed to take taxes from people they refused to represent. What came out was "embarazada."

Adrienne laughed so hard she had to set the orange down. "Charlotte. You just said the politicians are pregnant."

"They're what?" Charlotte's face went hot, and her hand shot out and knocked two of the index cards onto the garage floor, where they landed face down.

"Embarazada means pregnant," Adrienne said, wiping her eyes. "It's a false friend. It looks like embarrassed, but it isn't." She knelt and picked up the cards, tapped them square against the table, and slid them back to Charlotte's side. "Wilson did the same thing at his first debate. He told a roomful of exchange students that his father was constipated instead of embarrassed, and they laughed for a full minute."

From the doorway, where he'd been leaning with a glass of iced tea for who knew how long, Wilson said, "It was the longest minute of my life." He came in and dragged a lawn chair to the table. "Keep going. Don't restart. That's the whole trick. You apologize in the language and you keep going, and after that you stop being afraid of it."

Charlotte restarted the timer herself, which felt like a different kind of cheating, but she started again mid-argument, at taxes, and this time when she reached for embarrassed she paused, and said instead, "Deberían sentir vergüenza," they should feel shame, and the word held. Something loosened in her chest. She heard her own voice find a rhythm that wasn't English's rhythm, arguments arriving in an order she hadn't planned, the conclusion surfacing before the premises, which was apparently how the language liked to build a case.

But then a harder problem surfaced, one her English outline hadn't contained. She had planned to argue for lowering the age on the grounds that sixteen-year-olds are affected by policy, and are capable of judgment, and are already asked to be responsible. Listening to herself say it in Spanish, she found she half-believed the other side: that the vote is a lineage handed down, that its weight comes partly from its rarity, that a rite of passage might lose something by being moved earlier. She stalled. She stood at the folding table with the paint ring under her cards, caught between two arguments she could both defend.

"So?" Adrienne said softly, when the silence had gone on long enough. Her teasing had drained away; she was watching Charlotte the way you watch someone carrying something full. "Which is it?"

"Both, I think," Charlotte said, in English, because she had earned the break. "In Spanish it's clearer to me that I believe both." She looked at the cards, at their careful English, which now seemed obsolescent to her, a technology she had already outgrown for this particular purpose. "The part I can't decide is whether that's a real position or just refusing to choose."

"It's a real position," Wilson said. "Ms. Buchanan calls it a considered position. She says the ones who scare her are the ones with no doubts left."

Charlotte turned the timer over on the table, watching the numbers run without her. "Okay," she said. "But next time I say it in Spanish." She squared the cards, took a breath, and started again, this time from the middle.

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
knowledge_domain: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
fact: To find customers with no orders, a common SQL pattern LEFT JOINs customers to orders and keeps only rows where the orders' customer ID IS NULL.
story:
The public library on Alder Street kept its computer lab in the basement, beside the microfilm machines nobody used anymore, and it was there that Naomi sat on a Thursday evening with a notebook, a library card, and a problem she had promised to solve by Monday. Her mother's office was merging its customer lists, and someone had asked, almost as an afterthought, which customers had never ordered anything at all. Her mother had repeated the question at dinner with the particular helplessness of a woman who could read a balance sheet but not a line of code, and Naomi, who wanted very much to be the kind of person who said yes, had said yes.

The trouble was that she had said yes to a language she did not speak. She had spent two evenings watching videos and copying examples, and the examples kept finding things that existed: customers who had ordered something, sorted by name, joined to their orders. Every table in the tutorial world seemed to hold hands with every other table. Nobody showed her how to find an absence.

Harlow arrived at six with a paper cup of vending machine hot chocolate and the expression of someone conducting an inspection. "You've been down here for three hours," she said, dropping into the next chair. "You look like a ghost."

"I look like a person who is failing."

"You're not failing, you're marinating." Harlow spun the chair in a slow circle. "Lisa monetized a whole photo page last summer by just posting consistently for a month. You can do one spreadsheet."

"It's not a spreadsheet. It's a database, and the data's in two tables, and the customers I need are in the one where nothing happens." Naomi pulled the notebook toward her and read her own handwriting back to herself: customers in one table, orders in the other, and somewhere between them a silence she was supposed to retrieve. "Every join I try gives me the people who did order. I can't query people for what they didn't do."

Ms. Papadopoulos came down at some point to collect the abandoned microfilm reels, and paused behind them long enough to read the screen over Naomi's shoulder. She said nothing, only tapped the edge of the monitor twice with one knuckle, the way she did when a book a student claimed was not in the catalogue turned out to be shelved one row over. Then she carried the reels upstairs.

Naomi stared at the knuckle-mark afterward as though it were a clue. It was Lisa, later, on the phone with the sound of a party behind her, who said the careless and useful thing. "My cousin does this. He calls himself a savant, which is pernicious because he just read one book. Anyway he's always going on about some join where the missing side comes back empty. Like you keep the customer and the empty spot where the order should be." Lisa's voice dropped out under a wave of laughter, and Naomi wrote down: keep the customer, keep the empty spot.

She typed it slowly, half certain she was inventing grammar. LEFT JOIN, the customers to the orders, and then, in the place where a condition belonged, the words IS NULL, so that only the rows with that empty spot survived. She thought of it like laying two lists side by side and keeping everyone whose second column stayed blank. She ran it. The wheel spun. The screen filled with names.

There were forty-one of them, and the third one down belonged to her mother's boss. The man who had asked the question at the office, the one who had seemed so casual about it, had apparently never placed an order in the company's entire history, and Naomi understood at once, in the basement's fluorescent hush, why the question had been asked at all. Somebody upstairs wanted ammunition. Her innocent query had just manufactured it.

She saved the file, then sat without touching the keyboard, listening to the microfilm room hum. She had wanted to be the person who said yes, and she had said it, and the answer was now sitting in a document with a man's name in it, accurate and complete and not hers to interpret. She thought about deleting it. She thought about her mother's face at dinner, the tiredness under the question. She thought about how a query, once you learned to write it, would always tell the truth, and never once tell you what to do with the truth.

Harlow leaned over and saw the name. "Oh," she said quietly.

Naobia copied the file to a second drive, then a third, and put all three in her backpack, zipping it shut with the sound of a small decision being locked. On her way out she stopped at the front desk, where Ms. Papadopoulos was stamping returns.

"You knew," Naomi said.

"I knew the book was in the stacks," Ms. Papadopoulos said. "Section 005.7. What you found in it is your business." She slid one more stamp down, firm and even, and looked up. "Come back Monday. Tell me what you decided."

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
knowledge_domain: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
fact: An arbitration clause requires the parties to settle disputes through private arbitration instead of in court, and in the US it is often paired with a waiver of class-action lawsuits.
story:
The ceiling fans of the phone store moved the air without cooling it, and Robert stood at the counter holding his mother's cracked phone in both hands like something that had died. He had dropped it on the court two days after graduation, and now the screen bled green at the edges whenever it woke. He was leaving for college in three weeks. He needed a phone that worked, and he needed it on his own plan, the first contract with his own name on it, and he had the money from the summer job saved in a folder on his laptop at home, converted to cash in his pocket.

Noa, who had been in his grade until halfway through senior year and now wore a lanyard with the store logo, waved him over to the far terminal. "You're upgrading or starting fresh?" she asked, already pulling up the options. Robert said starting fresh, and Noa nodded and slid a tablet across the counter for him to review the plan while she fetched the demo unit from the back. She had always been the one who finished things, he remembered, the one who completed group projects the night they were assigned. He liked that she hadn't asked about the crack. He hadn't wanted to explain the game, or the rain, or his father watching from the fence and saying nothing.

The tablet showed the terms of service in small grey type, and because he was eighteen and had forty minutes before the bus, Robert actually read them. Most of it was boilerplate he half understood, liability and billing and consent gathered into numbered sections, but near the end a heading caught him: dispute resolution. He read it twice. The words said that any dispute would be settled through binding arbitration rather than in court, and that the customer waived the right to participate in a class-action lawsuit. He did not know precisely what arbitration was, but the shape of the sentence was clear enough: somewhere private, somewhere without a jury, instead of a courtroom.

When Noa came back, he turned the tablet toward her. "What's this part mean, that I can't sue and I can't join a class action?" She glanced at it and shrugged with real friendliness, not dismissal. "That's the arbitration clause. Most of them have it now." A man in a suit, Mr. Adebayo, the manager Robert guessed, paused behind her on his way to the register and looked at Robert with mild curiosity, but said nothing, and Robert was grateful for that.

He sat with it while Noa set up the transfer. On one hand the clause was a small thing, an inchoate worry about a dispute he would probably never have with a phone company; the phone was the concrete need, the thing underpinning everything else, his mother calling him at night in a new city, his roommate finding him at the airport. On the other hand he kept thinking about the word waiver, how many times in his life he had signed things without reading, permission slips and code-of-conduct forms, his signature scattered through the world like seeds he had never watched grow. He wanted his first real signature to be one he had read.

"Can I take the terms home and think about it?" he asked. Noa checked the clock. "The promo ends today," she said, and then, softer, "but I can hold one in the back till tomorrow if you want. We're not supposed to, but." She held his eyes a second longer than the sentence needed. He said yes, please.

He took the bus home and read the whole document on his laptop, and then, because he could not stop, he looked at the terms of the maps app on his mother's cracked phone, scrolling on the green-bleeding screen. There it was again, the same clause, the same waiver, in an account his father had set up years ago with a click of a box nobody had read. The whole family had already agreed to it, three times over, without knowing. Robert felt something in him settle, not into peace exactly, but into a decision: he would sign tomorrow, because the phone mattered and the risk was theoretical, but he would sign having read it, and he would keep reading, every time, which was not the same as protection but was something.

At dinner he told his father about the clause, and his father said, "So what did you decide?" and Robert said he had decided that most contracts you can't really refuse, but you can know what you're not refusing. His father chewed on that, then slid the housing packet for Robert's dorm across the table, the one he had co-signed in June while Robert was at practice. "Read page twelve," his father said, and pushed his reading glasses up his nose. Robert turned to page twelve and began to laugh, quietly, at the heading at the top of the page, which was exactly the one he had read that afternoon, word for word, already signed in his own careful hand.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Psychologist George Bonanno's research on bereaved people found that resilience is common, and that there are no mandatory stages that everyone must pass through after a loss.
story:
Mackenzie had agreed to spend Saturday at her grandmother's house mostly because nobody else would, and partly because she wanted the blue enamel kettle before her aunts divided everything into labeled freezer bags of grief. The house smelled like cardamom and dust, and every drawer she opened seemed to contain either rubber bands or photographs of people making the same face at the same lake in four different decades.

Rian came with her, which Mackenzie had not expected. Rian had been strange since the funeral two weeks ago, quieter at lunch, but still at lunch, still laughing at Riley's impressions of Mr. Silva's slow chalk technique, and something about that seemed to be bothering Rian more than the funeral itself had. Within an hour of arriving, while they sorted a shelf of china neither of them dared to wrap, Rian finally said it. "I think I'm doing this wrong. Grams is gone and I'm making jokes and studying for the chemistry test like it matters. My mom cries at commercials for yogurt. Shouldn't I be in a stage by now?"

Mackenzie held up a teacup with a hairline crack and considered the shelf above the stove, which her grandmother had declared off limits for thirty years. "There are stages, though. Everybody knows that. You're supposed to go through them in order, like a line at the DMV." She said it with confidence, the way she repeated most things adults had told her once, and Rian nodded miserably, which should have made Mackenzie feel better about her own composure and instead made her feel like a fraud.

They climbed onto the counter, because if the house was going to be sold anyway, the stove shelf's sovereignty had ended. Behind a tin of ancient saffron they found a battered paperback her grandmother must have bought used, because it had a stranger's ticket stub from a 2004 ferry inside it as a bookmark. The spine was cracked at a chapter about loss. Mackenzie read aloud while Rian steadied her elbow, and the author, a psychologist named George Bonanno, had done research on bereaved people and found that resilience was common, that most people were more resilient than the mythology of grief allowed, and that there were no mandatory stages everyone had to pass through after a loss.

There was also, further in, a sentence Mackenzie had to read three times, about how people tried to operationalize grief, to turn it into a checklist you could score, when really the researchers' own data kept refusing to behave. "That's me," Rian said. "I've been running my own little audit. Day one, denial, check. Day four, anger, nothing. I figured I'd failed the anger section." Mackenzie said, "You can't fail a section that doesn't exist," and then, because it was true and also terrible, "although now you have no excuse for your personality."

Rian threw a dish towel at her. They were both laughing, actually laughing, in the dead woman's kitchen, and Mackenzie caught herself watching the doorway for her grandmother, who would have been delighted and would have pretended not to be. That was the part nobody had warned her about, or maybe the part Bonanno had tried to warn her about: nothing stayed in its lane. She had spent two weeks performing a calm she believed was fake, doing homework, feeding the cat, and privately calling herself a monster in fairly specific terms, a kind of casuistry where she was both lawyer and guilty party. It had not once occurred to her that the calm might be real, and real did not mean shallow.

Down in the basement they found the reason the shelf was forbidden: five years of plum wine in unlabeled bottles, turbid and purple and faintly menacing, which explained a great deal about certain Christmas parties. Mackenzie held one up to the bare bulb. "We could dump these, or we could leave them for the buyers and let them think this family was interesting." Rian took the bottle from her, set it back in the row, and straightened the whole rank of them like little soldiers. "Leave them. She hid them for a reason. That's her last joke and we don't get to erase it."

Mackenzie took the kettle home in her backpack. In the car her mother asked how it had gone, and Mackenzie said, honestly, that it had been a good day, that they had laughed a lot, and she watched her mother decide not to be hurt by that, watched her almost succeed. She thought about explaining the research, about resilience and stages, but some things you had to find on a forbidden shelf yourself or they sounded like an excuse. Instead she said the kettle had a dent in it, and her mother said her grandmother had dropped it during the blackout of '98 and told the story every winter, and neither of them said anything for a while, and it was not a sad silence exactly, more like the kitchen after the kettle has just clicked off.

That night Rian texted a photograph of the chemistry study guide captioned "day fifteen, no stage, feeling great about it," and Mackenzie, lying on her bed with the dented kettle's lid in her hand like a small brass moon, texted back, "Bonanno says most people are like this." Then, before she could dress it up or doubt it, "I'm still sad though. Both things." Rian replied with a single thumbs up, and down the hall her mother's television went quiet, and Mackenzie got up to fill the kettle and turn on the stove.

activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
knowledge_domain: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
fact: The USDA advises reheating leftovers to an internal temperature of 74 degrees Celsius (165 degrees Fahrenheit).
story:
Nicolas stood at the steel counter with a printed page in front of him, a page he had made himself: seven dinners, a grocery list, a cooking order. Ms. Teo had assigned it two weeks ago. Plan a week of meals, she said, shop for it, cook in batches, eat like an adult. His list had chicken thighs on Sunday, a bean stew on Tuesday, rice to carry through both. He had costed it against his mother's grocery receipts and come out four dollars under, which he had not expected.

His partner for the unit was Alissa, who had already done her shopping and brought everything in a canvas bag, organized by aisle. Caleb was at the next station arguing with his own list, which had somehow included three kinds of cheese and no vegetables. Nicolas slid his page toward Alissa. "Tell me what's wrong with it."

She read it twice. "Nothing's wrong. That's what worries me." She tapped Sunday's column. "You cook all this rice for two dinners. Then it sits. Then you reheat it Thursday."

"So?"

"So my dad got sick once from old rice." She said it flatly, the way she said most things. "He was fine, but he spent a night he'd rather forget."

Nicolas had never thought of rice as something that could turn on you. It was inert, a background food, the thing his grandmother made in a dented pot every night of her life. But Alissa's father had a specific night he'd rather forget, and that was evidence, of a kind. He raised his hand.

Ms. Teo came over and he asked how you would know reheated food was safe. She didn't lecture. She opened the supply cabinet, took out a thin metal probe with a digital readout, and set it beside his cutting board. "The thermometer's the answer to that," she said, and walked off toward Caleb and his cheeses.

He poked it into the chicken as it rested and watched the numbers climb. The display settled and he wrote it down. The rice was the real question.
