He had cooked a double batch, spread it on a sheet pan to cool, portioned it into containers, and refrigerated two of them for later in the week. On Thursday, in class, he would pull one out and reheat it in the skillet, and he would not know, standing there, whether it was safe or only hot. Hot and safe were different things, and he had gone sixteen years without ever once distinguishing them.

He looked it up on his phone while the stew simmered. It took two searches. The USDA advises reheating leftovers to an internal temperature of 74 degrees Celsius, which was 165 Fahrenheit. He read it aloud, and Alissa said, "That's the number, then," and copied it onto his page in the margin, where his own handwriting had already started to look less certain than it had on Sunday. Caleb leaned over from the next station and asked what they were doing. Nicolas held up the thermometer. "Leftovers have to hit 74 Celsius to be safe," he said. "165 Fahrenheit." Caleb looked at his cheese, then at the thermometer, and asked to borrow it after them.

The cooking itself went faster than Nicolas had imagined. Because everything was planned, because the onions were all chopped at once and the chicken went in the oven while the stew built on the stove, he spent the hour moving instead of hesitating, and the unfamiliar efficiency gave him something close to exhilaration, a lightness in his wrists. He noticed his own attention sharpen and thought, distantly, that this was what people meant when they said planning invigorates rather than constrains. Then he burned the first batch of rice's bottom layer and revised the thought.

At home that weekend he cooked Thursday's container of rice in his mother's skillet and stood with the probe waiting for the readout. His mother watched from the doorway, arms crossed, half amused. The number crawled past 70, then 74, and held. He took the pan off the heat. "It's fine," he said, more to himself than to her.

What he couldn't resolve was the rest of it. Whether his grandmother's nightly rice, made fresh and never tested, had been luck or something he didn't understand yet. Whether Alissa's father's bad night proved a rule or only one kitchen. He had a number now, 74, and the number was solid in a way the rest of his knowledge wasn't. He washed the skillet and left the thermometer on the counter, probe out, where his mother would see it in the morning. She picked it up on her way to the coffee pot and turned it over in her hand.

"How much did this cost?" she asked.

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: In Kahlo's The Broken Column (1944), her spine is painted as a cracked Ionic column visible through an opening in her body.
story:
Luca had promised himself he would not write about the tears. Everyone wrote about the tears. The assignment sheet from Mr. Ivanova sat on the easel beside him like a summons: formal analysis, colour, composition, symbolism, no biographical padding, no feelings diaries. He had until Friday, and it was already Wednesday lunch, and the print of the painting propped against the classroom radiator was staring at him with those famous eyebrows, daring him to say something a thousand other students had not already said.

"Stop glaring at it," said Mikaela, dropping her bag on the taboret. "It's not going to apologize." She peeled a clementine with the concentration of a surgeon and offered him half. "Sunny's coming. He says he found a video where a guy compares her palette to a hospital."

"There's no way that's real."

"Twelve minutes, mostly about how green means she was sad, which, Luca, is exactly the essay you're about to write."

"She's got a crack in her, okay, and she's holding herself together with a corset, and there's a column where her spine should be, and nails everywhere, and the background is this cracked, dead land that goes on forever, like a desert that's given up." He heard himself and winced. "See. That's the essay. That's everyone's essay."

Sunny arrived with his phone already raised, breathless from the stairs, screen thrust forward. "Watch this bit. He says the nails are like that saint who got shot full of arrows. Sebastian. Look, they even lie the same way, all over the torso but not the face, because the face stays calm." He tapped pause on an image of a martyr painting, porcelain skin and small red wounds, arranged almost decoratively.

Luca looked between the two images for a long moment, clementine section forgotten in his mouth. That was the thing he had been circling all week without landing on it. The painting was not only a confession; it was a construction. The corset straps were drawn like ribbons on a package. The column had flutes and a scrolled capital, Ionic, an order from temples and banks and courthouse facades, set inside a body where it had no business being. He said the thought out loud, badly, then again better: "It's like she built herself into an altarpiece. The body as a church, the column as the spine holding up the roof. Except the column is broken, so the whole structure is a lie she's showing you on purpose."

"You just did the whole assignment in one sentence," Sunny said. "I hate you. Mine's going to be about how the video guy has a beard."

"Yours is on Rothko. You're fine."

Mr. Ivanova drifted over from the sink, drying his hands on a paint rag that had once been white. He looked at the print, then at Luca's notebook, which contained the words DEPOSITION? and igneous?? and a small drawing of a clementine. "You've discovered the hard part," he said. "Structure can be subject. Write that. And whoever put 'igneous' in their vocabulary list for this week, the ground in that painting is not volcanic rock, it is cracked earth, and you know it isn't if you look for two seconds."

"It's my list," Luca admitted. "Fine. Metaphorically igneous. Cooled from something molten."

"It's a metaphor if the reader can follow you," Mr. Ivanova said, and drifted away again, trailing turpentine.

Mikaela licked a strand of clementine off her thumb. "Okay, altar theory. But the column's Greek and the arrows-guy is Catholic and the corset is, what, medical? She's mixing everything. Your essay is going to be a museum gift shop." Luca laughed, because it was true, and then stopped laughing, because it was true in a way that might actually be the point. Maybe the mixing was not sloppiness but method, the way a deposition gathers testimony from witnesses who contradict each other and the truth sits somewhere in the seam between them. He wrote mixture as method and underlined it twice, then, on second thought, added a question mark. He could not yet say whether she had chosen the contradictions or simply lived inside them, and pretending otherwise would be the kind of essay the tears always got.

The bell for afternoon classes rang down the hall, a sound like a dropped tray. Mikaela gathered the clementine peels into her palm; Sunny pocketed his phone mid-video, the beard guy still explaining something in silence. Luca stayed one extra minute, looking at the print. The land behind her ran to the horizon in flat bands of ochre and grey, split by hairline fissures, so that she stood on ground that was broken exactly as she was, and no one had taught him that in any class; he had just now seen it. He picked up his pen and wrote, under the question mark, one more line: the earth has a spine too, and it is also cracked. He read it over, decided it was either the best sentence of his life or the worst, and left both possibilities standing.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Many Orthodox churches, including the Russian Orthodox Church, celebrate Christmas on January 7 because they keep December 25 on the older Julian calendar.
story:
Sebastian's grandmother lit the last candle on the table at four in the afternoon, when the sky over the snow already looked like wet slate. It was January 7, and the house smelled of fried fish, dill, and the particular dustiness of the good dishes that came out once a year. He had been at his grandparents' since noon, carrying chairs up from the basement and peeling potatoes while his mother argued with an aunt about whether the honey cake had risen enough.

The problem had started three weeks earlier, at school. Eloise had asked him, in the parking lot with everyone breathing steam, whether he had done anything for Christmas. He had said yes, automatically, because there had been a tree at his own house and a turkey and his father's terrible jokes. Then she had asked why his grandmother's Christmas, the one he had mentioned offhand, came after New Year's, and he had said something about tradition, something vague, and changed the subject to Alan's broken windshield. It bothered him that he had done that. He had lived inside this split calendar his whole life and could not actually account for it.

Now, at the table, he waited for the moment when his grandfather would stop moving and sit. When the old man finally lowered himself into his chair, Sebastian leaned over the kutya and asked, as casually as he could, why they did this on the seventh when the whole street had already taken their lights down.

His grandfather tore a piece of bread and considered it. "We keep December twenty-fifth," he said. "On the Julian calendar."

"The old one," Sebastian's mother added, from the far end, and then someone asked for the beets and the conversation slid sideways, and that was all the table gave him.

He turned it over while he ate. December twenty-fifth, but on a different calendar, one that ran behind the one on his phone, so that the date landed two weeks after the neighbors'. Many Orthodox churches did this, he was fairly sure; his grandfather had cousins who were Russian Orthodox, and they had sent a card that arrived after the holiday. The two weeks were the gap between the calendars, though nobody had said so in those words, and he did not push for more, because his grandfather had gone morose in the way he did when the subject circled back to the village, or to his brother, or to anything before 1991.

After dinner Sebastian was sent to the hall closet for more napkins, and there he found the wall calendar his grandmother still hung, the religious one with a saint in each corner. He ran his finger along the small squares. December 25 sat squarely in the middle of the page, and under it, in the fine print of the Julian reckoning, that same day was printed in the margin of January 7. So it was the same day, arrived at by an older count. He stood in the cold closet with the napkins under his arm, and the small grey square transfixed him for a moment, the way a word you have mispronounced for years does when you finally see it written down.

Earlier that week, in biology, Mr. Ferreira had drawn two circles on the board, one feeding on the other, and used the word parasitism while Alan whispered a joke about mistletoe that Sebastian hadn't caught until later. Sebastian thought about the two Christmases now, the one at his parents' house and this one, and decided that calling one a parasite on the other would be wrong, and cheap. The tree-and-turkey version had never fed on this; they just ran on different clocks, and his family carried both, and mostly nobody asked, and mostly he never had to say anything, which was maybe why he had never learned how.

He took the napkins back to the table, then stood in the doorway with his phone under his jacket and typed a message to Eloise. "Ok so I actually found out. We celebrate Dec 25, but my grandparents keep it on the Julian calendar, the old one, which puts it on Jan 7. A lot of Orthodox churches do it, like the Russian one. Two weeks after everyone else. That's the whole thing." He read it over once. It was accurate as far as it went, and it did not go very far. He did not know why the older calendar had been kept, or whether his own children would keep it, or which table he would someday be responsible for.

His grandmother appeared beside him with an empty tray and looked at the phone, then at him. "Help me with the tea," she said. He put the phone in his pocket, unsent, and followed her into the kitchen, where the kettle had just begun to sing.

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: Connecting words such as Spanish 'sin embargo', meaning 'however', let a debater signal a counterargument clearly even when the rest of their grammar is simple.
story:
Leo had volunteered for the Spanish debate before he understood what volunteering meant. Five minutes, entirely in Spanish, on whether cities should make public transit free, and he had eleven days to become the kind of person who could do that. He spread his notes across the library table by the window, three pages of vocabulary he'd copied from the textbook, and read them over and felt his stomach tighten in a way that was entirely somatic, a thing his body knew before his mind did.

"Give me one," said Tye, dropping into the chair across from him with a bag of chips he wasn't supposed to have in the library.

"Give you one what?"

"Argument. In English first, then your Spanish. I'll tell you if you sound like a robot."

Leo cleared his throat. "Public transit should be free because it reduces traffic and pollution." He tried it in Spanish. It came out flat, correct, a sentence standing alone in an empty room. Then the next one. Then the next. Each sentence arrived, said its piece, and left, and there was nothing between them.

"You sound like a list," Tye said, through the chips. "Like a guy reading parking regulations."

Miah arrived with her laptop and heard the last attempt. She pulled up a recording she'd made of last year's debate club final, a kid from the immersion program arguing about school uniforms. Leo listened. The kid's grammar wasn't much better than his, honestly. But every so often a word appeared that seemed to turn the sentence, and suddenly the kid sounded like he was answering an opponent who hadn't even spoken yet.

"What is that word," Leo said. "He keeps saying it. Sin embargo."

"It means 'however,'" Miah said. "Connecting words like that. Sin embargo, therefore, although. The immersion kids use them constantly."

Leo sat back. However. Such a small hinge, and it held a whole door. He looked at his three pages of nouns, transporte, contaminación, impuestos, and realized what was missing from them. He had bricks and no mortar. He tried it, haltingly. Public transit reduces pollution. Sin embargo, free transit costs the city money. Even with his simple grammar, the sentences leaned toward each other. It sounded, for the first time, like someone thinking out loud, like a person who had heard the other side and was not afraid of it.

"So you're going to build the whole thing out of that?" Tye said. "Six sentences and a bunch of howevers?"

"Maybe," Leo said, but the idea had already started turning. He'd been planning to argue that free transit was obviously good, the way you argue when you're sixteen and certain. But the word kept pulling at him. Sin embargo. However. If he couldn't say "however," he couldn't afford doubt, because doubt needed somewhere to stand. Now he had somewhere. He crossed out half his notes and started over, this time writing his opponent's best argument in the middle of the page, in Spanish, where he couldn't look away from it.

Mr. Byrne came by on his rounds and paused at the chaos of their table. He didn't shush them, which Leo took as a small mercy, since shushing was Mr. Byrne's primary instrument of order, wielded with the solemnity of something from antiquity. He only moved the chips bag six inches toward the trash and said, "The debate? I judged that once. The students who argued one side only never placed."

"Because the judges denigrate them?" Tye asked, pleased with himself.

"Because they gave us nothing to think about," Mr. Byrne said, and moved on.

Leo tested the shape of the thing. Five minutes, so roughly thirty sentences at his slow pace. He laid them out and counted the turns. He'd say free transit helps people who can't afford fares. Sin embargo, somebody pays, and the someone is usually the taxpayer, so a city has to decide whether the benefit is worth the cost, and honestly he did not know if it was. He'd say free transit might attract more riders. Sin embargo, more riders with no new buses just means crowded buses, and whether a city would build those buses was a question about money and political will, which was beyond what five minutes of his Spanish could hold. He liked that the word let him hold two ideas at once without pretending they fit together neatly. That felt, unexpectedly, like honesty rather than weakness.

"Say the whole opener," Miah said. "Timed."

He stood up, which felt ridiculous in a library, and started. His grammar stumbled and his accent was probably terrible and twice he lost a word and had to circle around it. But every time he reached a turn, he planted the word and the turn held, and he could see it land on their faces, the moment they understood which side of the argument he was about to leave behind.

"Two minutes forty," Miah said, clicking her stopwatch. "You're short."

"Short is fixable," Leo said. He sat back down and pulled the page toward him, pen already moving through the margin, adding a question he genuinely wanted the answer to, the one about whether people ride free buses they don't otherwise need, and how anyone would even measure that. Tye stole another chip. Somewhere behind the shelves, Mr. Byrne told someone, quietly, to put the book back where he'd found it.

"Again from the top," Leo said.

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: In countries with low death rates, a total fertility rate of about 2.1 children per woman is needed to replace the population without migration.
story:
Edouard spread his homework across the kitchen table: an atlas, a ruler, and a printout of a population pyramid shaped like an actual pyramid, wide at the bottom, narrowing to a point. Japan's was printed beside it, and Japan's looked like an upturned wine glass, thick in the middle, almost nothing at the base. The assignment asked him to decide, from the shapes alone, which country would need more primary schools in thirty years and which would need more nursing homes, and to justify the answer in two hundred words.

The radiator under the table ticked. His mother moved through the kitchen with laundry, paused at his shoulder long enough to read the title, and said, "Population," the way she said "Weather," which meant she considered the subject closed. She left. Edouard laid the ruler along Japan's base and discovered the bottom bars were shorter than the ones above them, which meant the youngest group was smaller than its parents. He wrote: fewer children now, so fewer parents later, so even fewer children after that. Then he crossed it out because it sounded like a threat.

He texted Samir. "Did you get the 2.1 thing." Samir replied with a photograph of his own page, half done, then a message: "no. why isn't 2 enough. 2 kids for 2 parents, that's level, that's obvious." Edouard stared at the wine glass. It did look obvious. Two for two, in and out, a seesaw balanced. But somewhere he had seen the number 2.1, and the point one had bothered him all evening, that small obstinate decimal, like a pebble in a shoe.

Mr. Brown knocked at the back door at seven with a casserole dish, because Edouard's mother had broken her wrist falling on the ice and the neighbourhood had organized itself into a rota without telling anyone. While she signed for the dish with her left hand, Mr. Brown looked over at the table. "Population pyramids," he said. "I remember those. Cold War geography, we all had to prognosticate the Soviet Union's future. Got that one wrong." He tapped Japan's shape with a knuckle. "Whatever you predict from that, you'll be retired before anyone checks your work. Handy field."

Edouard laughed, and after Mr. Brown left he sat with the phrase retired before anyone checks. There was something freeing in it. He flipped his notebook to a clean page and drew the pyramid for his own country, a shape with a slightly pinched waist and a base that had been thinning for years, the morphology of it familiar from the news without him ever having looked at it directly. The news called the falling birth rate a crisis, but the word crisis felt parochial, something shouted by people who had only ever seen one country's shape. On the page, his country and Japan were the same shape at different stages, one wine glass full, one still filling.

Anya called at eight about a history essay and stayed on the line while he worked. He told her about Samir's seesaw. "Two for two," she said, "except it isn't, because not everyone has kids, and some kids don't grow up, so you need more than two to keep it level." He wrote it down. "How much more?" "We looked it up in geography. In countries where not many people die young, it's about 2.1 children per woman, and that's the level just to replace the population without migration." He added the point one to his notes and felt the pebble leave his shoe. Two was a seesaw drawn in the air; 2.1 was the seesaw actually resting on the ground, where the math of real lives lived.

He wrote his two hundred words, then read them over. Fewer children at the base meant schools closing before nursing homes opened, but the timing he could not pin down, and he said so in the last sentence rather than inventing a number migration might make a fool of. He was aware this was the second time that week he had ended an assignment with an honest shrug, and that Mr. Brown would approve and the marker might not.

His mother came through again on her way upstairs, the laundry basket balanced against her hip, the cast on her wrist already marked with Samir's sister's signature and one small drawing. She stopped at the table. "So are we getting the schools or the nursing homes?" Edouard looked at the pinched pyramid of their own country, then at Japan's glass, and turned the notebook so she could see both shapes side by side. "Look at these," he said, "and tell me which one we are."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: For Mexico's Day of the Dead on November 1 and 2, families build home altars called ofrendas with orange marigolds, whose bright color and strong scent are believed to guide souls home.
story:
The church hall smelled of melted wax and cempasúchil, the orange marigolds stacked so thick on the tables that the scent reached the back pew where Hayden sat with his jacket still on. His mother had spent three days arguing with his aunt about whether they were doing this at all. His father had stayed home, not angry, just quiet in the way that meant he didn't know what to do with a grief that wasn't his. Hayden held the photograph flat on his knees, a picture of his grandfather in a borrowed suit at someone else's wedding, squinting into the sun.

The altar took up half the transept. Candles in glass jars, pan de muerto with its sugared knobs like finger bones, a clay figure of a dog, paper flags cut into lace and strung overhead so they turned slowly in the heat of all those flames. Beside him, Makenzie was copying the labels on the photographs into her phone, because she was writing about it for the school paper and had never heard of any of this before tonight. "Every family does this at home too," she said, reading from a pamphlet someone had given her at the door. "Home altars, for November first and second."

"Ofrendas," said Tomas, appearing behind them with two paper cups of coffee. His family had helped build the altar; his mother had wired the marigold garlands along the railing of the choir loft. "That's what they're called. My mom builds one every year, even here, even now." He said it without ceremony, the way he said everything, and wandered off toward the folding chairs where his little brothers were fighting over a piece of the bread.

Hayden looked down at the photograph. His grandfather had died in March, between the ice storm and the census forms, and Hayden had not cried at the funeral and had not cried since, and this bothered him in a low, persistent way, like a dripping faucet in another room. He had come tonight mostly because his mother had asked, and partly because Makenzie wanted company, and partly for a reason he could not have named in homeroom on Monday: he wanted to find out whether any of this reached a person who was gone.

Tomas's mother waved him over to the altar to help arrange the last flat of flowers. Hayden followed, carrying his photograph like a dish he was afraid to drop. Up close the marigolds were almost too much, a saturated orange that seemed to hum, and the smell was sharp and green beneath the sweetness of the bread. "Why these and not roses," Hayden asked, and Tomas shrugged and said he'd asked the same thing when he was eight. "The color and the smell. They're supposed to guide the souls home. That's the whole idea. That's why there's a path of petals from the door."

Haydan looked back toward the entrance. There it was, a scattered line of orange petals on the tile, running from the doors through the nave to the altar, and he had walked over it without seeing it. He felt something loosen in his chest, not sorrow exactly, closer to exhilaration, the kind that came before you understood what you were feeling. He placed the photograph on the table between a wedding picture and an army portrait, weighted the corner with a candle jar so it wouldn't curl.

Makenzie found him there a few minutes later. "Can I quote you?" she asked. "For the article. Somebody whose family is doing this for the first time." Hayden considered the request. Half of him wanted to lambaste the whole idea of turning the night into copy, six hundred words with a photo caption, grief as content. The other half remembered that Makenzie had driven forty minutes to be here, that she had asked his mother's permission before taking any pictures, that she had teared up at the dog figurine and pretended she hadn't. Both halves were true, and he let them stand next to each other the way the photographs stood on the table, not arguing, just occupying the same surface.

"You can quote me if you don't make it neater than it is," he said. "I don't know if I believe the flowers lead anywhere. I know my grandmother believed it, and my mother half believes it, and I put the photo up anyway." Makenzie wrote none of it down, which surprised him, and then said, "That's the quote. I'll remember it." Above them the paper flags turned, their shadows moving across the altar like something arboreal, like light through leaves, though the nearest tree was three blocks away in the dark.

His mother came to stand beside him. She put one hand on his shoulder and the other on the table's edge, near the photograph but not touching it. The candles guttered in a draft from the doors, steadied, and held. Down the aisle of petals, someone new came in, shaking rain off an umbrella.

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: Lynn Hunt's 1984 book Politics, Culture, and Class in the French Revolution turned attention to symbols, language and festivals as sources for understanding the Revolution.
story:
The essay was due Monday morning, and Thomas had brought three books and no argument to his grandfather's house, where he was spending the last weekend of the summer. The prompt asked how views of the French Revolution had changed since 1800, which meant he could not simply write about the Revolution. He had to write about the writing about the Revolution, a hall of mirrors his teacher had warned was easy to get lost in.

His grandfather's study smelled of pipe tobacco that no one had smoked in a decade. On the third shelf Thomas found a paperback with a cracked spine, a survey from the 1960s, and read a paragraph that described the Revolution as the triumph of a rising middle class, a story with a clear hero and a clear direction. In the margin, in his grandfather's small handwriting, was one word: "Too neat."

On Saturday morning Jocelyn texted him from the historical museum two towns over. She worked the front desk and wanted the weekend hours, but the place was empty and she was bored. She sent a photograph of a reproduction poster from 1793, a woman in a red cap holding a pike, with the words LIBERTÉ OU LA MORT beneath her feet. Underneath, Jocelyn had typed: "Come look at this, it's weird and French, isn't that your thing."

Alek drove him over because Alek wanted to see the museum's display case of vintage pocket watches, which he intended to sketch for the portfolio due to the art school on the same Monday. This was Alek's own deadline, and he carried a sketchbook under his arm like a passport.

The poster hung between a case of buttons and a printed copy of the Declaration of the Rights of Man. Thomas stood in front of it for a long time. He had been treating images as decoration, the kind of thing a textbook used to fill space. But the woman's red cap, the pike, the slogan in enormous letters: someone had chosen those, printed thousands of them, pasted them on walls where frightened people walked past. He copied the caption into his notebook, and the caption cited a source. He read the citation twice. "Lynn Hunt's 1984 book, Politics, Culture, and Class in the French Revolution," he said aloud. "That's the one Mr. Nikolaidis mentioned. It turned attention to symbols, language and festivals as sources." He had assumed, in class, that the mention was an aside. Now he wrote it at the top of a fresh page.

Jocelyn leaned over the desk. "Sources for what?"

"For understanding the Revolution itself. Not just what the assemblies decided, but what the songs and the festivals and posters meant to the people marching in them." He took a photograph of the poster, then crouched to photograph the caption.

She tapped the frame. "Then you should come back at three. A guy from the county archive brings out the festival programs on Saturdays, the ones nobody looks at. He likes an audience."

At three o'clock the archivist, a thin man with a lanyard, laid out facsimiles of programs from the Festival of the Supreme Being: processional routes, choir instructions, a diagram for a cardboard mountain. Alek, who had finished two watches and needed a third, sketched the mountain diagram instead. Thomas photographed everything, and on the drive back he talked so much that Alek told him to save it for the page.

That night he assembled the essay at his grandfather's desk. The older story, he wrote, had excoriated the Revolution's later violence as a betrayal of its promise, or defended it as necessity, but either way it had treated politics as the only real subject. Then a newer scholarship had widened what counted as evidence, reading symbols, language and festivals alongside laws and factions. Thomas drafted a paragraph arguing that the second approach was not mere relativism, not a shrug that said every view was as good as another, because it demanded more evidence, not less. He deleted the sentence and wrote it again with the poster in it, the pike and the red cap and the slogan, and it held better.

There was one thing he could not settle. Whether the newer view had gotten the Revolution more nearly right, or simply asked a different question, he could not say, and by midnight he decided not to pretend otherwise. He wrote that much plainly, as a limit rather than a flourish. Then he printed the draft, left it under a book on the corner of the desk, and went down the hall to see whether his grandfather, who was still awake, remembered buying that paperback, and why he had written "too neat."

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: Schenck v. United States introduced the 'clear and present danger' test, allowing speech to be punished if it created a clear and present danger of harm Congress could prevent.
story:
Ashton had told everyone, more than once, that the mock court didn't matter to him, that he was only filling the slot because Mr. Campbell had asked, and by the fourth time he said it he almost believed it. The courthouse smelled of floor wax and old paper, and the courtroom itself, a borrowed annex with the real judge gone for the day, was cold enough that his hands had gone stiff around his notes. He was the only student assigned to argue both sides of the same case, which Mr. Campbell had called an exercise and which Ashton privately called a punishment. In twenty minutes he would stand up and defend the school's right to punish a student's speech, and then, after a recess, he would stand up again and eviscerate every argument he had just made.

Heather found him by the water fountain, chewing a pen cap. "You look like you're about to throw up," she said.

"I'm fine. I never get nervous." He said it evenly, and it was true in the version of himself he preferred. His stomach disagreed, quietly, and he ignored it the way you ignore a dog scratching at a door.

The bench of student justices filed in, Maci among them in a black blazer she'd borrowed from her mother, and the room settled. Ashton rose for his first argument. He had built it around the oldest tool he could find in his research, a test from a case called Schenck v. United States. "Under Schenck," he said, and his voice came out steadier than he'd expected, "speech can be punished if it creates a clear and present danger of a harm Congress could prevent. The school argues the student's speech created exactly that kind of danger." It landed well. Maci's pen moved. He sat down feeling something dangerously close to triumph.

Three weeks earlier, he had been in his kitchen at eleven at night, a printed case summary going soft at the corners where his damp fingers had held it, reading the same sentence over and over. His mother had come down in her robe and asked what was wrong, and he'd said nothing, school stuff, because the truth was harder to arrange into a sentence. The case he'd been given was a fictional one, invented for the competition, but its facts were close enough to something real that he'd had to close the folder and stand in the dark pantry for a minute, breathing the smell of cardboard and coffee grounds, before he could keep reading. That night he had decided to master both sides so completely that neither one could surprise him. He had told himself it was strategy.

In the second round, the student arguing against him, a boy from another school with a voice like a radio announcer, stood and swung at Ashton's foundation. "Schenck is a hundred-year-old test," the boy said. "Nobody argues like that anymore. My opponent dragged in an antique because the modern standard wouldn't help him." A murmur went through the benches. Ashton felt his ears go hot. He had known Schenck was old; he had not known everyone else would know it too.

When his turn came, he stood with the recess still ringing in him, the taste of fountain water metallic on his back teeth, the overhead lights buzzing at a pitch he'd never noticed before. Here was the moment he could patch over the damage, invent a bridge, bluster. Instead he heard himself say, "Schenck introduced the clear and present danger test. My opponent is right that it's old. But it's also true that it allowed speech to be punished if it created a clear and present danger of a harm Congress could prevent, and that logic hasn't vanished; it's been refined, not erased." He looked at Maci. "I'd rather argue from the old test honestly and let this court decide what it's worth than pretend I never found it."

Maci leaned forward. "So which do you actually believe?"

The room waited. He had rehearsed two answers, one for each side, and both were fluent, and both, he understood suddenly, were incomplete in the same way. "I think the danger test protects more speech than people assume," he said slowly, "and less than free speech absolutists want. I think the same words can be a threat in one room and nothing in another, like carbon being graphite or diamond depending on how it's put together, same element, different form." He'd learned that word, allotrope, in chemistry, and it had never fit anywhere until now. "I can't tell you which form this student's speech took. That's the part I genuinely don't know."

He sat down. His heart was loud and he was grateful nobody could hear it. Later, in the hallway, while the justices deliberated, Heather bought him a vending machine granola bar and said, "You argued both sides. Which one was you?" Ashton peeled the wrapper down and looked at the window at the end of the corridor, where the real courthouse steps were bright with afternoon light and people he'd never meet were going up and down them, saying whatever they wanted, most of it harmless, some of it not. "The last part," he said. "The part where I said I don't know." Somewhere behind the deliberation door, a chair scraped.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: The legal age of consent differs by country and even between US states, and in many places it falls between 16 and 18.
story:
The flashcards were spread across the kitchen table like a failed card trick, and Isabella had been rehearsing for an hour before Joanie finally pushed the kettle aside and sat down. "Okay," Joanie said, "explain it to me like I'm an idiot." That was the deal. Ms. Ahmed had asked for two student facilitators for the peer health session, and Isabella had volunteered before she understood what she was volunteering for, which was standing in front of thirty sophomores on Thursday and talking about consent, contraception, and how to get tested at the clinic on Marsh Street without needing a parent's signature. She could recite the facts. What she could not do yet was say them out loud, in order, to a face.

"Consent is a yes that's freely given," she began, "and it can be taken back at any time." She heard her own voice flatten into the flashcard cadence, the one that put people to sleep. Joanie watched her with her chin in her hand, half mesmerized, half gone. "You sound like a pamphlet," Joanie said. "Say it like it matters." Isabella started over, tried to sound like a person, overshot into something too casual, and felt the whole project wobble between logos and something warmer she couldn't name. She wanted to be accurate, and she wanted to be kind, and the two kept elbowing each other.

Holden came in through the back door with his shoes still on, phone in hand, interrupting the contraception run-through, which up to that point had consisted of Isabella naming methods while Joanie guessed failure rates like a game show. "Listen to this," Holden said, dropping into the third chair. "That case in the news, the teacher in, wherever it was, Portugal or somewhere. The article says the age of consent there isn't what it is here." He squinted at the screen. "It's sixteen there. Different country, different law." Joanie said, "I thought there was just, like, one rule." Holden shrugged. "Guess not."

Isabella took the phone and scrolled, and then, because the article mentioned it in passing, she looked further, and the further she looked the less single the rule became. "It's not just countries," she said slowly. "It differs between states here. Ours is one thing, the state over is another. In most places it falls somewhere between sixteen and eighteen." She had been building Thursday's session on the idea that there was a floor everyone stood on, a number, a line, and now the line turned out to move depending on where you were standing. Joanie leaned over her shoulder. "So which number do we tell them?" "The one here," Holden said, like it was obvious. Isabella wasn't sure it was obvious. The law here and the law somewhere else could both be true at once, and a room full of fifteen-year-olds deserved to know that the ground shifted.

She tried the section again, folding it in. "Consent has a legal side and it has a real side," she said to Joanie, practicing. "The legal age of consent differs by country and even between states, so you have to know what it is where you live. But the part about freely given, that doesn't change." Joanie nodded, then ruined it by saying, "You're doing the pamphlet thing again." Isabella laughed, which was the first honest sound of the afternoon. She flipped the flashcards face down. Maybe the logos had to come with a story, something that had happened to someone, something she half knew and half invented.

Then Joanie, quiet for a moment, said the thing that had been sitting under the whole rehearsal. "Do you know how to get tested? Like actually, for yourself?" The kettle ticked as it cooled. Isabella knew the clinic's address, its hours, the fact that appointments could be made without a parent, and she did not know whether she could walk in there herself, say the words out loud to a stranger, sit in the waiting room with her own name on the clipboard. Holden looked at the table. "I could drive you," he said. "Not because you can't. Just so it's less of a thing." "It would be more of a thing," Joanie said, "but maybe that's fine."

Ms. Ahmed would have told her, if asked, that a perspicacious facilitator admits the limits of what she knows, but Isabella hadn't asked anyone. She was figuring out Thursday on her own terms: she would give them the clinic's number and the facts about consent, and she would say plainly that the age of consent was not one universal number but a range that depended on where you lived, between sixteen and eighteen in many places, and that they should check their own state rather than trust a rumor. What she could not promise the sophomores, or Joanie, or herself, was that knowing all of it made any of it easy. Some of them would sit in that waiting room and be terrified anyway. She would probably be one of them, someday soon, which was either the best qualification or the worst.

She gathered the flashcards into a stack and squared the edges against the table. Joanie picked up her keys and Holden still had Isabella's phone, thumbing through the clinic's website, and outside the kitchen window the streetlight came on too early, the way it always did in November. "Thursday," Joanie said at the door. "You'll be good. Just not like a pamphlet." Isabella held the stack against her chest and said, "More like a person who read a pamphlet."
